Another such enigma is the vault particle . A vault particle is a large, hollow protein shell found in nearly all the cells in our body. It was discovered in 1986 by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha, but its function remains elusive. At roughly three times the mass of a ribosome, it’s one of the largest known molecular complexes in eukaryotes—organisms with complex cells, such as mammals (as opposed to simple, usually single-celled “prokaryotes,” such as bacteria). Vaults take their name from their shape. When observed under an electron microscope, the ribbed shell reminded Dr. Rome and Dr. Kedersha of the vaulted ceiling of a cathedral. In mammals, the shell is made of 78 copies of the major vault protein, arranged as two identical halves joined at the middle. Vaults are found across most of the eukaryotic tree , from slime molds to humans, so scientists believe that they must do something useful. Researchers have proposed various functions, including transporting molecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm , protecting cells from toxic compounds such as cancer drugs , and supporting innate immunity , but none of these proposals have been conclusively confirmed. Other studies have shown that mice lacking vaults still survive , which suggests that vaults may be necessary only under specific environmental conditions. Still, the question remains: why would evolution retain something so large if it didn’t have an important function? Interested in whether Claude could help make progress on this long-standing open problem, our biology research team has been investigating vaults. We haven’t yet determined their biological function, but we did find that many more vault proteins across the tree of life, including those in prokaryotes and the bacteriophages that infect them, can assemble into complete vault-like particles. Related proteins had already been found in the genomes of both prokaryotes and phages, but to our knowledge no one had shown that they assemble into vaults. A vault in a prokaryotic cell gives researchers a simpler system to study. Compared with mammalian cells, bacteria are quick to grow, which makes it easier to investigate where vaults came from, what their basic structure looks like, and what, if anything, they contain. Studying the bacterial relatives of human proteins has been informative before. Bacterial versions of cGAS–STING signaling , gasdermins , and viperins revealed the microbial origins of these human immune defenses. In those cases, their function in humans was already known. For vaults it is not, and their prokaryotic relatives may help reveal it. Here, we describe how we uncovered the molecular structure of a vault from a bacteriophage . Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. Like all viruses, they hijack their host cells to make their proteins, so this vault would be built inside a bacterium, a prokaryotic cell. The vault is built from 96 copies of a single protein, compared with 78 in human vaults. By duplicating part of the protein, we engineered the vault to be even larger. Together, these results shed light on how such complexes assemble and suggest how they could be adapted for biotechnology —for example, as nanocapsules for delivering enzymes . The cap of the L05 vault. (Left) the whole vault, imaged by cryo-EM. (Right) its cap seen from above. All 48 chains wind in from the rim toward the tip, overlapping as they go. Two-thirds continue past the first tier and one-third reach the tip, so the cap narrows like a stepped dome. This work also demonstrates our team’s wider aim: to speed up research in fundamental biology by building Claude into every step of the process. Under our direction, Claude searched protein databases, designed the DNA constructs, optimized the isolation method, and processed the microscopy data. As a result, a vault purification that conventionally takes three days took us about 90 minutes, and a first structural model was ready 34 hours later, which we estimate would normally have taken us weeks. Despite this progress, there is still much to be learned about these perplexing structures. When we shared the structure with Dr. Rome, whom we brought on to advise us on this research, he said: Figuring out the function of vaults is still enormously challenging. I am pleased that Anthropic has so much good data. Now, other people will be working on this problem … The broadness of Anthropic’s finding[s] suggests that it is going to be a complicated function and an interesting ride. Our lab is releasing these findings early to continue to show the scientific community how Claude can be used for discovery. You can read more about our results and methods in our preprint , and we will be releasing the structures and additional data soon. A vault-like structure in prokaryotes We uncovered the vault structure using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), in which many copies of a particle are flash-frozen and imaged with an electron beam, before being combined into a single 3D model. The vault is built from 96 copies (48 copies per half) of a single phage protein, which we call L05, with a combined mass of about 9.5 megadaltons . By contrast, the mammalian version has 39 copies per half. The phage-derived vault is also shorter and wider: roughly 54 nanometers long and 45 wide, compared with 67 by 40 in mammals. Despite being shorter, it encloses about 25% more volume because it is more spherical. The protein chain that makes up its wall is built from seven repeating segments stacked end to end, rather than the nine in mammalian vaults, and its end caps are flatter. It’s among the largest protein shells ever identified in prokaryotes. One notable feature of its structure is how the caps close. A wall 48 copies around must narrow toward the pole, and it does so in three steps, like a tiered dome. In every group of three neighboring copies, one ends at the first step, one at the second, and one continues to the tip. The three copies are identical along the wall, but take different shapes (conformations) in the cap. Given that we can make this vault in the lab and isolate it quickly, we also experimented with altering its structure to learn more about how these proteins assemble. Working with Claude, we made 15 altered versions of the protein, most with changes at the points where neighboring copies touch. Some single changes near the cap were enough to prevent the shell from closing: in place of sealed vaults we saw open, rosette-like particles, which shows that this region is needed to seal the shell. We also tried making the vault even bigger. Ordinarily, the wall is built from seven repeating segments. When we copied two of them, giving the protein nine—the same number as in the human vault—it assembled into even larger vault particles, increasing the enclosed volume by approximately 20%. These experiments demonstrate how vaults could have changed size over their evolutionary history by duplicating pieces of their own wall without disrupting how they assemble. The L05 vault (left) beside an engineered version (right) with two extra segments in every copy, both by cryo-EM at the same scale. The added repeats make the vault longer and wider. Finding, isolating, and mapping a new vault with Claude Part of the reason vaults have remained unexplained for 40 years is that they are missing from the organisms biologists rely on most for genetic experiments, including baker’s yeast, fruit flies, and nematode worms. In mice, which do have vaults, animals that are bred without a vault partner protein or the vault RNA develop normally, leaving no obvious defect to follow up. In recent years, bioinformaticians identified distant relatives of the vault protein in prokaryotes, but it wasn’t clear whether these proteins formed vaults. Our team set out to answer that question. The research required several steps: surveying genetic sequences to find where vault proteins occur across the tree of life, producing and isolating the most promising candidates to test whether they actually assemble into vault-like particles, and determining the structure of one of the particles to see how its chains fit together. We began by using Claude Science to search for the vault protein’s relatives across a database of about 15 billion predicted proteins. They turned out to be rare but widely distributed, present in 29 major groups (phyla) of bacteria and four of archaea (the other main group of prokaryotes) but in less than 1% of species with a sequenced genome. We then chose 44 of these proteins and tested each in a cell-free system to see which genes yielded full-length protein and how much. We chose the proteins, and Claude turned each protein sequence into DNA tailored to the host cell, added the control sequences that switch a gene on, and prepared the designs for ordering. We moved the best performers into living E. coli bacteria, where 15 of 24 produced soluble protein. Next, we needed to isolate the particles. The conventional method, developed for eukaryotic vaults, spins the sample through a tube of increasingly dense sugar and takes approximately three days. To speed this up, we decided to try size-exclusion chromatography. In this process, the sample flows through a column of porous beads. In a process called fractionation, small molecules get stuck in the pores, while the vaults, which are too big to enter, come out first, in what’s known as the void volume. Claude first argued against taking the chromatography approach, because clumps of misfolded protein come out in that same void volume. We went ahead anyway, and Claude helped make it work by recommending a specific column as well as methods to track the vault protein and check whether particles had formed. Claude then proposed loading the contents of ruptured cells straight onto the column with no purification beforehand. We were reluctant at first because these columns are expensive, and the raw contents of ruptured E. coli cells can clog them or cause contamination. But we were willing to test an unconventional idea, and it worked. We are not the first group to isolate vaults on sizing columns , but our optimized method takes about 90 minutes from cells to microscopy grid instead of days. Under an electron microscope, seven of the 15 proteins had assembled into vault-like particles. Cryo-EM confirmed the vault shape for four of those seven, two from phages and two from bacteria. We chose one of the phage proteins, L05, for the detailed structure described above because it was among the best at forming complete, closed particles. Determining a biomolecular structure often takes weeks or months of manual work with specialized software. We directed Claude through the whole process. Working in an internal multi-agent harness with access to internal compute resources, Claude set up an open-source processing software (RELION) and ran each step, while we advised on the analysis decisions. A first full model was ready in 34 hours, and the final maps were ready about a week after processing began. Cryo-EM of L05 vaults made in E. coli : a field of particles (large panel), selected single vaults (bottom), and 2D class averages in which the ribs of the wall are visible (right). Claude also pointed out a feature of the structure we can’t yet explain. A pocket partway up each of the 96 protein copies holds a small molecule that shows up clearly in the map but that we haven’t been able to identify. Claude found that its shape resembles coenzyme A, a common helper molecule that cells use to shuttle chemical groups around. If it is coenzyme A, or something similar, it would be an early hint at a possible function. A new way of doing science For us, this was a dramatically different way of doing science. None of us had worked with a protein assembly this large, and we had limited experience in structural biology. We took the project on anyway, because Claude could make up for what we didn’t know and rapidly perform analyses that would otherwise have taken us much longer. In under four months, we screened dozens of candidate vaults, prepared samples for the microscope, and solved the first vault structure found in prokaryotes. Most of this work could be achieved by a typical lab with access to existing Claude products. Only the cryo-EM analysis, which used hundreds of GPUs in parallel to save time, required more computing resources than might be available to an academic institution. Working this way also showed us where Claude needed improvement. A protocol it wrote called for a growth medium containing an additive that interferes with getting DNA into cells, which set the project back by two weeks. Early in the cryo-EM processing, it skipped a standard step and produced a flawed map blended with its mirror image, and we told it to stop improvising (“Please let’s do normal things unless they don’t work”). We have used what we’ve learned to inform Claude’s development. We shared our lab notes with the ML researchers who train Claude, so they could see where the model went wrong. This has informed the kind of data Claude learns from. Over the course of the project, Claude got much better at these tasks as new models arrived, making seemingly fewer errors in DNA construct design and better identifying potential pitfalls in experiments. In areas we knew well, we caught mistakes quickly, but they cost us time in areas we didn’t. Overall, we found that the benefits of working this way far outweighed the drawbacks, and Claude has become integral to our work. So far, we have made these vaults only in E. coli , and have yet to test whether they form in the bacteria and phages where they’re naturally found. More work is needed to determine the function of these particles, and our work only deepens the mystery. As Dr. Rome put it: Will we find out that they are all doing the same thing? Or will we see an evolutionary development of vault function? Maybe they are doing the same thing as human vaults, and that is also very interesting. We will continue our research into the function of vaults, and will share more as this work progresses. Work with us We are releasing the details of our work in our preprint . If you have an idea for what these vaults might be doing, or a system in which to test it, we would like to hear from you: mdurrant[at]anthropic.com , nicholasp[at]anthropic.com . Authors & acknowledgements Contributors Januka Athukoralage, Peter Yoon, Nicholas Perry, Matthew Durrant, and the Life Sciences Team at Anthropic Disclosure: Dr. Rome was a paid consultant, providing feedback on the manuscript.

items.summary: Algorithms and theory Google’s mission presents many exciting algorithmic and optimization challenges across different product areas including Search, Ads, Social, and Google Infrastructure. These include optimizing internal systems such as scheduling the machines that power the numerous computations done each day, as well as optimizations that affect core products and users, from online allocation of ads to page-views to automatic management of ad campaigns, and from clustering large-scale graphs to finding best paths in transportation networks. Other than employing new algorithmic ideas to impact millions of users, Google researchers contribute to the state-of-the-art research in these areas by publishing in top conferences and journals. But integrating MDE into SfM remains challenging. Unlike classical triangulated sparse pointclouds, MDE produces dense depthmaps with significantly higher error variance. Inspired by modern RANSAC estimators, we propose a Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (MBA) to accommodate MDE error variance with its density. With MBA, we show that MDE depthmaps are sufficiently accurate to support SoTA or competitive results in Structure-from-Motion and camera relocalization. CL adapts the Training Impulse (TRIMP) model by leveraging continuous heart rate and movement data from wearables, enabling minute-level intensity estimation. We also discuss the derivation of weekly target loads, intended to guide fitness maintenance. METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted on 31.2 million hours of wrist-worn wearable data collected over a six-week period. The dataset comprised a 40,000-subject subset (37.9% female) of consenting Google Pixel Watch® users in the United States, aged 18 to 80 years (18-39: 41.8%, 40-59: 43.5%, 60+: 14.6%). Measured data included minute-interval heart rate averages, resting and maximum heart rates, minute-interval averaged accelerometer log energy, and manually-logged or auto-detected activity types. Cardio Load scores and target loads were calculated daily for each subject and compared across age and gender. We also compared the proportions of CL gained during workouts and incidental daily activities for these groups. Median weekly Cardio Load (CL) values exhibited consistency for individuals between 30 and 75 years of age. When analyzed in five-year age groups, the coefficient of variation (CV%) of median weekly CL values within this age range was less than 4.5%, with younger and older subjects demonstrating higher and lower median CL, respectively. The median proportion of CL accumulated during structured workouts versus incidental daily activity was 41.0% (female) and 49.0% (male) for all subjects, though this varied considerably with average weekly workout duration. CV% of weekly target load and daily target load over 6 weeks was 23.6% and 35.2% respectively. CONCLUSION: Cardio Load provides a continuous quantification of activity load from wearables, acknowledging both structured workouts and everydayincidental activity. CL is equitably rewarded for age ranges spanning 30-75 years. Weekly target loads were found to have little measurement variability and be more consistent and, consequently, more practical for planning training and physical activity than daily targets. This "knowledge latency" forces employees out of self-service workflows and into costly support ticketing queues. This paper introduces SENTINEL, a geo-contextual AI framework designed to shift enterprise support from reactive retrieval to proactive interception. The architecture employs a novel dual-engine system integrated into an omni-present interface. The first engine utilizes Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct pre-emptive, historical case-grounded audits of documentation, generating a "Contextual Density" score that identifies friction zones. The second engine is an autonomous Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) agent that surfaces in-situ via a location-intelligent assistant window, resolving queries in real-time. By functioning as a strategic "defensive barrier" at the point of origin, SENTINEL demonstrates how a proactive AI assistant can drive high-fidelity, in-situ case deflection. items.content: The Industrial Alliance for Semiconductors gathered its members in Brussels to take stock of the Technology Sovereignty Package and launch the European Chip Design Platform. © Nikola Ilic On 4-5 November, the Industrial Alliance for Semiconductors , in collaboration with the European Commission, met in Brussels for the second time since the launch of the Technology Sovereignty Package five months ago. Policymakers, industry leaders, researchers and Alliance members discussed the Chips Act 2.0 and how Europe can turn political ambition into industrial capacity. The event hosted the official launch of the European Chip Design Platform (EuroCDP) on 4 November, in the presence of Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen. The Commission is mobilising around €500 million in public investment for the Platform, together with Member States. It is a flagship initiative of the Chips Act to support a new generation of European chip design start-ups. EuroCDP is a cloud-based one-stop shop giving start-ups access to design tools, IP blocks, design enablement services, manufacturing capacity, training and finance. Early-stage start-ups working towards a seed round can receive grants of up to €100,000, and more mature companies may receive up to €16 million public funding. The programme also featured a high-level discussion with MEP Olivier Schenk, the European Parliament’s rapporteur on the Chips Act, alongside Killian Gross from the European Commission , bringing together institutional perspectives on Europe’s semiconductor ambitions. Discussions during the event explored the breakthrough innovations, leadership and talent needed to strengthen Europe’s semiconductor ecosystem, scale cutting-edge technologies and develop the skills required to compete globally. A dedicated session on physical AI examined how advances in computing, sensing and connectivity can enable the next generation of connected applications, and how Europe can accelerate their transition from technology development to industrial deployment. The programme also explored how growing demand for semiconductors in AI, cloud computing, high-performance computing, telecommunications and strategic infrastructure can translate into technology roadmaps and market opportunities. In this context, participants discussed the demand accelerators concept proposed under the Chips Act 2.0 , which aims to better align semiconductor supply with the needs of downstream industries and support the deployment of European technologies. Last update 5 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.title: Commission launches Education and Skills package to tackle declining basic skills, rapid digital change and teacher shortages

items.content: Today, the European Commission presents a new Education and Skills Package to reverse the decline in basic skills, help schools make AI and digital technologies work for learning and address teacher shortages. © M.photostock The package focuses on four priorities: raising achievement in basic skills, harnessing digital and AI tools for education, strengthening the teaching profession and making vocational education and training (VET) more agile, strategic and better connected. It also reflects changing labour market needs, which must be better addressed in education systems to safeguard Europe´s competitiveness and democratic resilience. Better and safer use of digital technologies for education On 3 November, the Commission established the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium on Education (EDU-EDIC) , at the request of eight founding Member States. The EDU-EDIC will enhance European tech sovereignty in education and pool resources and expertise to deploy trusted AI and digital services for schools, enable secure data exchange between education institutions, and help European education technology (EdTech) companies better serve schools across borders. This strengthens Europe's own capacity and tech sovereignty in education. President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen , said: “A stronger Europe starts with empowered young people. We are backing our Member States to raise standards in literacy, maths, science, digital and citizenship education. While also equipping children with the skills they need to safely navigate AI. And for this it is essential that they are supported by well-trained teachers. Together we will work to ensure future generations thrive.” Read the full press release . Last update 5 November 2026 Print as PDF

items.title: Make America Healthy Again
items.summary: Make america healthy again President Trump launched the Make America Healthy Again initiative to confront chronic disease, improve nutrition, and lower healthcare costs. This year, the administration advanced reforms targeting childhood health, food quality, and preventive care while increasing transparency and accountability in healthcare systems. These actions are laying the foundation for a healthier, stronger America. By prioritizing prevention over treatment and empowering families with better information and choices, the administration is addressing the root causes of poor health outcomes. These efforts are improving quality of life, strengthening communities, and ensuring a healthier future for the next generation of Americans. items.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. PODCAST SERIES Ideas Listen as members of the research community at Microsoft discuss the beliefs that animate their research, the experiences and thinkers that inform it, and the positive human impact it targets. Listen now Opens in a new tab More than a decade of work For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab) , but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Phalanx (opens in new tab) , in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea. Nova (opens in new tab) , HyperNova (opens in new tab) , NeutronNova (opens in new tab) , Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost. Brakedown (opens in new tab) , in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. Spice (opens in new tab) , Lasso (opens in new tab) , Nebula (opens in new tab) , and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor. Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second . More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab) , a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab) , which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together. Magnetar Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once. Figure 1. Magnetar proves a program’s execution and returns a small proof that anyone can check, with security resting only on standard hash functions. It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Looking ahead Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust . If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab) . Opens in a new tab Related publications Spartan: Efficient and general-purpose zkSNARKs without trusted setup Magnetar: High-speed post-quantum RV64 zkVM from standard hashes Neo and SuperNeo: Post-quantum folding with pay-per-bit costs over small fields Meet the authors Srinath Setty Senior Principal Researcher and Manager Learn more Research Areas Programming languages and software engineering Security, privacy, and cryptography Related labs Microsoft Research Redmond

items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. PODCAST SERIES Ideas Listen as members of the research community at Microsoft discuss the beliefs that animate their research, the experiences and thinkers that inform it, and the positive human impact it targets. Listen now Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. Listen now Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. items.content: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars: Synthetic enterprise environments : simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation Figure 1: Components of Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ? In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. Synthetic enterprise environments Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve. Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. These environments are scalable baselines that teams and organizations can build off of however they want. They are designed to exhibit the same structural and behavioral properties that make enterprise AI evaluation meaningful. Grounding in real world signals To ensure our synthetic environments are realistic, we grounded them in publicly available real world data sources. O*NET data from the U.S. Department of Labor’s occupational database was used to make synthetic employee roles and responsibilities realistic, calibrate the mix and frequency of work activities assigned to different roles, and tailor industry specific workflows such as clinical trial reviews or portfolio updates. Online job postings provide realistic role titles, reporting hierarchies, and departmental compositions. SEC filings inform organizational scale, business unit structures, and financial contexts. All of these sources are publicly available and have been reviewed and approved by Microsoft’s legal and policy organization. Figure 2: Real signals from public datasets that are used to ground the evaluation data generation Importantly, these synthetic environments are not static snapshots. They simulate dynamic, time-evolving organizations with meeting histories, project timelines, email threads that develop over weeks, and organizational changes that unfold naturally. This temporal dimension is essential because a large class of Copilot queries are inherently time aware. Questions like “What did the team decide last Thursday?” or “What’s changed since the last quarterly review?” only produce meaningful evaluations if the underlying data has a genuine temporal structure. Industry specific simulation We generated three synthetic environments across multiple industries, each with distinct characteristics that mirror real world usage: A pharmaceutical environment that includes regulatory submission workflows, clinical trial discussions, and cross functional safety review meetings A capital markets environment featuring deal pipelines, compliance communications, and client portfolio reviews An IT/software company that simulates sprint planning, code review discussions, and product launch coordination Figure 3: Industries targeted for industry evaluation data generation This industry specificity ensures that our evaluation queries test Copilot against the kinds of questions real users in those domains actually ask, rather than relying on generic test cases that may not surface domain specific failure modes. Automated query generation While synthetic environments provide the substrate for evaluation, they face a key limitation: we still need realistic evaluation queries. These are the questions that test whether Copilot can surface the right information, synthesize it correctly, and present it helpfully. Manually writing thousands of grounded, industry specific queries is prohibitively expensive and slow. That’s where our automated pipeline comes in. The six-stage pipeline Figure 4: Query customization pipeline that turns generic query templates into realistic, industry-specific queries We built an automated pipeline that turns simple, generic query ideas into realistic, industry-specific questions for Copilot. It starts with a large library of common workplace tasks, narrows them down to what’s relevant for a given industry, and adapts them using domain-specific language and context. The system then uses AI to generate queries grounded in the synthetic environment’s data, rewrites them to sound more natural and human, and validates each one for accuracy and uniqueness. The result is a rich set of high-quality, lifelike queries that enable scalable and reliable evaluation of Copilot across real-world scenarios. Validating synthetic quality Of course, generating synthetic data is only part of the challenge. We also need to ensure the data is good enough to produce meaningful evaluations. We assess synthetic environment quality using our internal semantic evaluation framework which measures quality across three dimensions: Structural fidelity : Does the organizational structure reflect realistic reporting hierarchies, team sizes, and cross functional relationships? Contextual relevance : Are the queries and workflows representative of actual enterprise usage patterns? Behavioral realism : Do the simulated users exhibit human-like communication patterns and collaboration dynamics? Content safety : Is the generated content free of harmful, offensive, or personally identifiable material, and does it avoid impersonating real individuals? End-to-end automation While our synthetic environments and query pipelines provide the methodology, they face several practical limitations without proper automation, including: Reproducibility : Manual processes produce subtly different results each time, making it difficult to compare evaluations across releases. Scale : The number of industry verticals and configuration variants exceeds what any team can reasonably produce by hand. Iteration speed : Manual creation takes days, delaying essential feedback and slowing down development cycles. Cross-team consistency : Without standardized tooling, different teams produce evaluation datasets with incompatible formats and quality levels. This automation reduced evaluation dataset creation from a multi-day manual process to automated runs. We estimate savings of approximately $100,000 per evaluation dataset and $300,000 in total project savings. But the more important outcome is that any team can now regenerate an evaluation dataset from the same configuration and get identical results. Microsoft Research StorY OptiMind: When the system meets the floor A three‑month pilot in a Midwestern bottling plant shows what happens when AI moves beyond chat and into decision-making, where constraints shift, stakes are real, and answers must hold. Learn more Opens in a new tab Privacy and safety by design Enterprise grade evaluation demands more than good methodology. It requires a privacy posture that allows teams to move fast without compromising user trust. A non-negotiable design principle of our industry evaluation datasets is that no real customer data is used at any stage of the pipeline . Every element, from organizational structures to email content to meeting transcripts, is synthetically generated, with no customer data inputs. Because the data is both fully synthetic and safety-screened, teams can share and reuse it widely without introducing reputational, compliance, or Responsible AI risk. Our safeguards include privacy preserving aggregation techniques where real-world statistical distributions are referenced, expert legal review and approval of all public data sources, and clear data provenance and lineage tracking throughout the pipeline. This means teams across Microsoft can use these evaluation datasets freely for experimentation, benchmarking, and regression testing without privacy review overhead or data handling restrictions that would otherwise slow down iteration. The privacy design is not a constraint on the system. It is what makes broad adoption possible. Results and impact Since starting this project, we have observed significant improvements across multiple dimensions. On synthetic data quality , our internal scoring system showed significant quality gains in the structural, contextual, and statistical fidelity of the generated data. Across our composite quality metric (which measures how closely synthetic data mirrors the complexity and patterns of real enterprise environments), scores improved 39% compared to our initial generation approach. Some industry-specific environments reached quality scores above 0.9 out of 1.0, demonstrating that domain focused generation produces highly realistic evaluation environments. The improvements were obtained in part by incorporating realistic, industry signals and in part by automating quality improvements via key composite quality metrics that help improve the structural integrity, contextual coherence and statistical diversity of our synthetic industry environments. On scale and efficiency , each synthetic environment now contains hundreds of users with complete communication histories across three industry verticals. Evaluation dataset creation has gone from multi-day manual effort to automated pipeline runs. On organizational adoption , our industry evaluation data generation platforms have been published to an internal shared catalog for cross-team reuse and established as the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. The difference wasn’t just incremental. It was a shift in how teams approach evaluation: from ad hoc, manual processes to standardized, reproducible infrastructure. Conclusion As we continue to expand what Microsoft Copilot can do, from single turn Q&A to agentic multi-step workflows, our commitment to evaluation remains at the heart of our approach. In enterprise AI, quality isn’t just about accuracy or speed. It’s about trust. Organizations need confidence that AI systems handle their information correctly, and that confidence can only come from thorough, repeatable evaluation. That trust rests on two commitments woven through everything we build: rigorous privacy protection and proactive content safety. Looking ahead, Microsoft Copilot is tackling even more exciting evaluation challenges: How do we assess the quality of multi-turn agentic interactions? How do we extend synthetic environments to capture organizational dynamics evolving over months or years? How do we build evaluation frameworks for AI systems that take actions, not just generate text? These are the kinds of questions our team is working on next. At Microsoft, we’re not just building AI. We’re building the infrastructure to ensure it works reliably for every enterprise, in every industry, at every scale . Thanks to everyone who’s worked on Industry Evaluation Datasets ! As they interact with the tools and systems around them, they adapt their reasoning and behavior to achieve their task. The adaptability of agents is what makes them so powerful, but they are goal-oriented and may not prioritize safety in pursuit of their objectives. It is the foundation of the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for building safe AI agents. OpenShell treats agent workloads as untrusted throughout execution. An agent is given access to what it needs, when it needs it. OpenShell has four key components: Gateway: The control plane that manages sandbox lifecycles and policies Supervisor: Checks outbound requests against policy and mediates access to credentials. This runs completely separate to the sandbox Sandbox: Isolates the agent workload and restricts filesystem and process access Policy prover: Adds formal verification, checking whether a policy’s permissions stay within an organization-defined ceiling. As the agents evolve, these components provide the infrastructure controls that allow them to work safely. Figure 1. NVIDIA OpenShell and NVIDIA Sentry, shown with a BlueField-4 DPU, connect an agent harness with knowledge, tools, and models in a secure agentic AI architecture. Supervisor middleware lets you inspect, block, or change the content that an agent sends and receives over the network as an additional enforcement layer. Gateway interceptors let operators add deployment-specific governance to OpenShell control-plane operations without modifying the gateway. Organizations also need to establish who an agent acts for, what authority it holds, and whether an action fits the task. Identity, authorization, data protection, and auditing each address part of that problem. OpenShell provides enforcement points where those systems can be integrated. They need high-bandwidth fabric and memory to keep those cores fed with the live data agents depend on. They need massive I/O to move data at speed between CPUs, GPUs, storage, and network. They need hardware-enforced security, because agents increasingly operate on sensitive enterprise data and must be isolated from each other and the host. They need to deliver all of this within the power envelope of a modern data center (more agent work per watt, not just more raw performance). NVIDIA calls this combination the max single-threaded CPU at scale , and NVIDIA Vera is built for it: massive Olympus cores, a second-generation Scalable Coherency Fabric, LPDDR5X memory, Gen 6 I/O, confidential computing, and an energy-efficient design purpose-built for power-limited data centers. Third, up to 1.2 TB/s of LPDDR5X memory bandwidth, with up to 40% lower loaded memory latency than chiplet-based designs, keeps agents supplied with the live context they need without stalling on memory access. LPDDR5X also makes Vera dramatically more efficient: Vera delivers 2x more performance per watt than x86 CPUs, while the LPDDR5X memory subsystem itself draws an order of magnitude less power than competing DDR5-based memory configurations, enabling more agent work within the same power envelope. Agent workloads depend on sandboxes: isolated execution environments where agents run code, invoke tools, and complete tasks without interfering with each other or the host system. The denser and faster those sandboxes spin up, the more agent work a given infrastructure footprint can sustain. For deployments that require additional protection, that separation can also extend into purpose-built silicon. NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs provide a hardware-isolated trust domain outside the agent’s reach. In the OpenShell reference architecture, BlueField-4 sits in the I/O path between agents running on Vera and the models they access. When it detects a threat or policy violation, BlueField-4 enforces policy in silicon, allowing NVIDIA Sentry to quarantine the agent within milliseconds. Together, they add an optional hardware safeguard alongside OpenShell’s software boundaries. Learn more about NVIDIA Sentry in this technical deep-dive . Vera provides the compute, memory bandwidth, and I/O to sustain those workflows. OpenShell supplies the runtime boundaries that determine which actions execute and which resources agents can reach. Together, Vera and OpenShell make secure agent execution a foundation for scale. Agents can run longer, use tools, and work with enterprise data within policies enforced outside their control. For deployments that require additional protection, NVIDIA Sentry on BlueField-4 adds independent monitoring and in-silicon enforcement. The NVIDIA Vera Rubi n platform , where LLMs run, together with OpenShell and NVIDIA Sentry on BlueField-4, are the pillars of the OpenShell reference architecture. They form the complete stack for safe AI agents: a complete, hardware-rooted foundation that gives organizations the performance to make agents productive and the controls to keep their work within authorized boundaries. items.content: Back to Articles Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software Enterprise Article Published October 29, 2026 Upvote 34 +28 Kate Soule katesoule Follow ibm-granite Luis A Lastras GrizleeBer Follow ibm-granite Subhajit Chaudhury subhajit1412 Follow ibm-granite Abraham Daniels abedaniels Follow ibm-granite Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1 , showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint. Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood. Updated Granite Speech ASR model — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass. Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set. While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy. This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon. Until then, test out our latest models , and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo. items.content: Back to Articles Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms Published October 29, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 21 +15 Mattt mattt Follow Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do. Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive. In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap , we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model. Today we're announcing two packages: AnySpeechRecognizer implements Apple's new speech-to-text API with a choice of recognition engine, including NVIDIA's Parakeet and Alibaba's Qwen3-ASR running locally on Core ML, and adds speaker diarization to track who speaks when. AnyDecisionModel answers yes-or-no, multiple-choice, and rating-scale questions with typed results and probabilities. It derives each answer from the model's probabilities instead of generating text, using a model on your device with MLX, Core AI, or llama.cpp, or a decision model from Jev or Ollama. Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.
