items.content: Back to Articles Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language Enterprise Article Published November 3, 2026 Upvote 18 +12 Praveen Venkateswaran praveenv Follow ibm-research Anupama Murthi anupamamurthi Follow ibm-research Hamid Adebayo harmedox Follow ibm-research Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other. Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it. Why decks are hard for small models A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at. It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from. It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent. There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them. Build it like a human: a designer and a coder Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter: The designer reads the plan and writes a structured JSON brief: the palette, the type system, and for each slide its layout, its exact content and a short design rationale. The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the pptxgenjs JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning. Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster. We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×. Synthesizing decks and their reasoning There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides. Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example: "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance." The coder reasons about geometry: "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart." The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example. The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest. What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions. Steering a deck in plain English Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives , short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]] : ## Rollout plan - March: pilot with two teams - May: security review complete - July: rollout to all of engineering - September: company-wide launch - November: first adoption review [[make this a timeline]] The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead. The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase. Category Example directive Layout [[make this a timeline]] Tone [[be candid, no spin]] Audience [[this is for the board]] Order [[lead with the ask]] Leaving out [[no pricing]] Emphasis [[highlight the headline number]] Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive. Building a check-and-repair harness Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first. Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned. First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code. The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse. Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right). To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average. Evaluation We evaluate on PresentBench , which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper. Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean. Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model. PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close. What's next The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training. We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling ) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining. What we learned Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts: Put the reasoning in the data. Training on why a choice was made, including what was rejected, teaches more than the choice alone. Fix the examples before adding a rule. When the teacher got something wrong, our first instinct was to add a rule to its prompt, and that rarely helped. The teacher copied its reference decks far more than it followed instructions, so fixing the reference was what actually changed its output. Make repairs safe by default. A fix that's kept only when it measurably helps can run on every output. Build the checker first. It's what makes the data trustworthy and the outputs safe to ship. items.content: Back to Articles Transformers Model Integration Contracts Published November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 15 +9 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months. When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it. Why bugs reach main Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels. The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main. Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB. This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU. Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine. Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main. Introducing Model Integration Contracts transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts: a fixture : the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned a usage path : a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step baselines : the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines. A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic . For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt: inputs = tokenizer( "The capital of France is" , return_tensors= "pt" ) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 4 , do_sample= False ) new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:] print (tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens= True )) It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md . A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later. On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes. The UMT5 regression We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28 . Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20. One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint. We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup. The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details. How models are shrunk The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear. The recipe now has four steps: Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds, including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers. Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible. We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name. Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte. Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test. Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds. Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR. We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail. The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style. Building MICs with agents Our CLI, tmic , creates the contract and builds the fixture. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months. When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it. Why bugs reach main Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels. The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main. Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study , the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB. This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU. Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine. Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main. Introducing Model Integration Contracts transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts: a fixture : the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned a usage path : a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step baselines : the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup. items.content: Back to Articles New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation Enterprise + Article Published November 5, 2026 Upvote 11 +5 Pranjali Joshi PranjaliJoshi Follow nvidia Rick Z rickznv Follow nvidia Yao Xu yaoxuhf Follow nvidia Qianli Ma qianlim Follow nvidia Chen-Hsuan Lin chenhsuanlin Follow nvidia Ming-Yu Liu mingyuliutw Follow nvidia Xiang Li ryanxli Follow nvidia Zhengfei Kuang zhengfei-nvidia Follow nvidia Zhonghao Wang zhonghaow Follow nvidia Jiaxiang Tang ashawkey Follow nvidia TL;DR NVIDIA Cosmos world model development platform adds four new open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family for generating interactive world simulation and multi-sensor multi-view driving scenes: 🌦️ Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto : Generate multi-view driving data with varied weather, lighting, and time of day. 🚗 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto : Stream synchronized camera and LiDAR observations for driving simulation. 🎨 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer : Turn simulator controls and a text prompt into photorealistic video. 🤖 Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual : Predict video from robot or camera actions. All four models are post-trained examples of Cosmos 3 Nano and have 16B trainable parameters. The models use OpenMDW1.1, permitting commercial and non-commercial use under its terms. Download the checkpoints · Read the technical report . Watch the demos Why do you need these checkpoints? 🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations. 🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds. 🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together. 🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short. Build Autonomous Vehicle Worlds with Cosmos3-Nano 🌦️Transfer-Auto: driving scenarios → multi-sensor data Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes, and supports joint RGB–LiDAR generation. Per-camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls specify scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance. Developers can vary environmental conditions to expand training and evaluation coverage, with optional initial RGB images to anchor scene appearance. Joint LiDAR generation additionally uses aligned HD-map range-map controls. Transfer-Auto also serves as the foundation for adapting Cosmos to your own sensor rig and driving domain. Start by post-training it on your data to accommodate your camera layout, LiDAR configuration, and target environment. The adapted model can be used directly for offline data generation or undergo causal training and few-step distillation for fast streaming simulation—the development path used to create Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto. Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto Prefer a notebook? Open Transfer-Auto . 🚗Sim-Auto: driving controls → streaming observations Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer-Auto. It generates successive small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in just a few denoising steps, using generated history and updated driving controls to support fast streaming and long, interactive rollouts. Provide per-camera captions and synchronized WSM controls, optionally adding initial RGB images. For LiDAR generation, include HD-Map range controls aligned with the camera controls. The distilled model generates successive chunks using its rolling history. Closed-loop interaction requires a simulation runtime and WSM renderer to update those controls from driving inputs. For a new sensor rig or domain, adapt Transfer-Auto first, then distill it into Sim-Auto. Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto Prefer a notebook? Open Sim-Auto . 🎨 Sim-Transfer: simulator controls → RGB Your simulator computes motion, contacts, and physical state. Sim-Transfer uses its spatial controls and a text prompt to render color observations that a policy can consume. Action → simulator update → spatial controls → generated RGB → next policy action Depth: relative distance from the camera. Segmentation: regions and object boundaries. Edges: scene contours. Blur: coarse appearance and layout. Text guides appearance; physics and ground-truth state stay with the simulator. Depth control to video Segmentation control to video Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer Prefer a notebook? Use Transfer . 🤖 Sim-Bimanual: actions → video Input Frames Output Video From Sim-Bimanual Simulation Checkpoint Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual simulates how an environment evolves in response to a bimanual robot’s actions. It supports interactive two-arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or human-operated joysticks. Start with an image, move the robot or camera, and generate the next observations. One control sequence can switch between viewpoint changes and manipulation. The mixed-action example uses 59 control values, padded to 64 during training. Its schema defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains. Follow those conventions so each value describes the intended motion. Keep timing aligned: T transitions need T+1 observations. Training transforms raw captures into the model’s action representation; released inference actions are already normalized. Here, Sim-Transfer generates visuals from a physics simulator’s updated state; Sim-Bimanual generates the next observation directly from the scene and robot actions. See the data contract and action schema . Requirements: Linux, an NVIDIA GPU, Docker, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit. The published vLLM-Omni setup was tested on one GB200; this is not a minimum-memory specification. The server downloads weights; the clients fetch sample inputs. Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual Prefer a notebook? Open Bimanual How streaming generation works Cosmos 3’s Mixture-of-Transformers backbone connects separate text-processing and visual-generation networks through attention. The generator predicts each short segment from the prompt, available controls, and generated history. Controls + history → generate chunk → decode images → update history Denoising refines noisy, compressed video representations into a segment. Temporal-causal attention lets it read available history and controls while blocking future target observations. A key/value cache retains attention information for the next prediction. The model operates on compressed video representations called latents. After the initial image, each latent time step represents four RGB frames. Transfer predicts one step per chunk; the optimized Bimanual setup in the report predicts two. Smaller chunks let new controls affect generation more often. The four-stage training recipe Stage 0 — Bidirectional adaptation: learn the domain and its control-to-video relationships from complete recorded clips. Stage 1 — Teacher forcing: predict each chunk from earlier recorded observations and available controls, with the clean answer and future targets masked out. Stage 2 — Consistency distillation: use a frozen teacher to train a student that generates each chunk in four denoising steps. Stage 3 — Self-forcing: train on the student’s generated history. A frozen teacher and an auxiliary score model supply the distribution-matching signal. Why the final stage matters: a slightly mispredicted object becomes context for later frames, so errors can compound. Self-forcing exposes training to that generated history. Distillation and caching reduce the cost of producing each observation. 🛠️ Adapt with your data The post-training recipes start from Cosmos3-Nano or compatible base weights and cover all four stages. Keep full training checkpoints to resume; exported inference weights omit optimizer and other training state. Transfer-auto : Post-train on your driving data to adapt to your sensor rig and domain, and generate offline synthetic data. Sim-auto : Apply causal training and distillation to an adapted Transfer-Auto model for fast streaming simulation. Sim-Transfer : Post-train the checkpoint for your environment with local data preparation, stage configurations, and resume. Sim-Bimanual : Post-train for your embodiment with data validation, stage configurations, checkpoint handoffs, and export. Give your coding agent the skill and dataset location. Follow the environment checks, validate a sample, and test training and restart before a longer run. Evaluate quality on held-out episodes: a successful short run verifies execution, not convergence. items.content: Back to Articles A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks. Published November 5, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 21 +15 Olesia Krizhevich olesiagradium Follow gradium Laurent Mazare lmz Follow gradium Eric Bezzam bezzam Follow Eustache Le Bihan eustlb Follow Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you. We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard. Why a voice should live on your device Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate. Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both. We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design. Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages. What we released Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio . Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes. It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now . Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license. Demos and first projects The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page. The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one. Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it. Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face. How Phonon did on the Hugging Face Open TTS Leaderboard The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub , the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility ( word error rate of the outputs ), speed ( inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio ), and naturalness ( UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean ). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most. On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish , and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size. Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio. Inference We built a new inference framework, ptts , specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®). Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile , e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself. It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs. Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer , held by the processor next to the text tokenizer: from transformers import AutoProcessor, GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration model_id = "gradium/phonon-31m-en" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) model = GradiumPhononTTSForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map= "auto" ) print ( f" {model.num_parameters():,} " ) # 30,788,354 print ( f" {processor.audio_tokenizer.num_parameters():,} " ) # 10,305,313 A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices . from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download from safetensors.torch import load_file path = hf_hub_download( "gradium/phonon-voices" , "voices/LMDIYE0Oa377Qh6Z.safetensors" ) voice = load_file(path)[ "speaker_wavs" ][ 0 ].T # (num_frames, 512) The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs: conversation = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [{ "type" : "audio" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Hello from Phonon." }]} ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, tokenize= True , return_dict= True , add_generation_prompt= True , processor_kwargs={ "audio_prompt_latents" : [voice]}, ).to(model.device) # prompt: <|audio_prompt|> × num_frames, "Hello from Phonon.", <|audio_bos|> generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio: outputs = model.generate(**inputs) # audio_latents: (batch_size, num_frames, 32) audio = processor.decode(outputs.audio_latents, outputs.audio_latents_mask) processor.save_audio(audio, "phonon.wav" ) See the docs 🤗 for more! What's next Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio . Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device. We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need. Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks. Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build. Schoellig , Andreas Krause , Max Simchowitz , Andrew Wagenmaker View a PDF of the paper titled Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement, by Michal Korniak and 23 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings - where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task - which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment - targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously - and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models. Schoellig Andreas Krause \BIGAND Max Simchowitz Andrew Wagenmaker Affiliation: ETH Zurich Affiliation: Technical University of Munich Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Affiliation: UC Berkeley Affiliation: Amazon FAR Affiliation: Physical Intelligence * Co-First Authors, order by coin flip † Co-Principal Investigators ‡ Lead Principal InvestigatorsProject page: https://lasgroup.github.io/generalist-improvement Repository: https://github.com/lasgroup/generalist-improvement Abstract The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings – where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task – which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment – targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously – and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Scaling the number of RL training tasks enables generalist improvement of generalist robot policies. As training task diversity increases, critic-guided policy extraction (OGPO) or refinement (BoN) prevent forgetting and improve performance on unseen tasks on MolmoSpaces , unlike filtered supervised fine-tuning (FSFT). Generalist robot policies, particularly Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs), have shown promise in enabling general-purpose robotic capabilities, allowing a single policy to be deployed across diverse tasks ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) . However, despite encoding diverse task-solving behaviors, such policies often lack sufficient reliability for robust deployment, and a degree of adaptation is typically necessary for effective performance ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2025b ; Reuss et al., 2025 ) . While enabling this adaptation through human supervision is often prohibitively expensive, autonomous adaptation through reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising approach to scale policy improvement, enabling robots to learn from their own experience in deployment ( Intelligence et al., 2025a ) . Yet, such autonomous improvement is typically limited to narrow single-task settings. As such, while these approaches enable generalist policies to improve, they may also specialize this improvement to the particular deployment task considered, and achieving improved performance on additional tasks of interest generally requires further online interaction and fine-tuning. A generalist policy, however, can produce a wide range of behaviors across diverse tasks, even if these behaviors may be far from optimal. Ideally we might hope that, by deploying on a diverse range of tasks, we could improve the performance of the policy across all tasks simultaneously – boosting its performance not just on a single deployment task, but on the entire distribution of tasks of interest. In particular, we might hope to enable truly generalist improvement : improvement on both the diverse set of tasks we deploy on, as well as generalization beyond these deployment tasks and improved performance on future novel deployment settings. This motivates the central question we consider in this work: how can we leverage interaction across a diverse set of tasks to enable online generalist improvement of generalist policies? That is, can a careful adaptation phase over multiple tasks enable both (i) improvement across these tasks simultaneously, and (ii) generalization beyond them, improving performance on tasks not encountered during post-training? In this paper, we undertake a systematic study to quantify generalist policy improvement across different axes of generalization. We show that appropriate recipes, when instantiated carefully, can enable not only generalist policy improvement across a diverse set of training tasks, but also task-generalization – improvement on tasks not seen during training. Further, we show that this improvement scales with the number and diversity of tasks trained on, as we showcase in Figure 1 . Our results suggest that moving beyond the single-task paradigm is not only possible but also crucial for achieving broader, generalist improvement. We isolate the essential algorithmic ingredients that enable multi-task learning and generalization. Specifically, we compare three families of learning approaches: (a) Direct Policy Adaptation , which directly improves the policy via filtered supervised fine-tuning on successful trajectories ( Peters and Schaal, 2007 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Qin and Springenberg, 2025 , FSFT,) . (b) Critic-Guided Test-Time Refinement , which uses test-time optimization against a learned state-action critic to improve actions. Here, we focus on Best-of-N sampling ( Nakamoto et al., 2024 ; Giridhar et al., 2026 , BoN,) with respect to that critic’s induced action ranking as a representative recipe. (c) Critic-Guided Policy Extraction , which updates a policy so as to maximize the value the critic assigns to the actions produced. Here, we adopt off-policy generative policy optimization ( Patil et al., 2026 , OGPO,) as a representative recipe, while also ablating alternative approaches such as combining FSFT and BoN sampling, or using AWR-inspired policy updates ( Peng et al., 2019 ) . Overall, while all three approaches enable some degree of generalization given a sufficient diversity in training tasks, we find that critic-guided methods enable a substantially greater degree of task generalization than direct policy adaptation alone . In particular, we show that critic-guided methods afford generalization both across training scenes, and, perhaps more surprisingly, across object types. Furthermore, we find that critic-guided policy extraction (OGPO) significantly outperforms test-time refinement (BoN), while also exhibiting similar scaling trends with training task diversity. This finding further points to critic-learning as the key component that enables generalist robotic policy improvement as task diversity scales. In addition to investigating algorithmic choices, we also systematically evaluate the training task distribution necessary for achieving such generalist improvement. We show that both the number of distinct training tasks, as well as the type of diversity exhibited in these training tasks, is critical to achieving generalist improvement. In particular, we find that a high degree of diversity in the required solution strategies within the training task distribution is crucial to learning generalizable task-solving behaviors. We believe these results illustrate a path forward for efficient online improvement of generalist robot policies. Rather than expensive single-task improvement on each deployment task of interest, our results show that, by amortizing this cost across a diverse set of tasks, one can enable generalist improvement, achieving improved performance on future deployment tasks of interest without paying the cost of additional online fine-tuning. 2 Related Work VLA post-training. Diffusion and flow-matching provide expressive generative policy classes that, when trained through behavior cloning at sufficient scale and diversity, can form the basis of generalist policies ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Reed et al., 2022 ) . Recent RL fine-tuning methods directly optimize such policies ( Psenka et al., 2024 ; Park et al., 2025b ; Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ; Patil et al., 2026 ; Li and Levine, 2026 ) , but scaling them to large VLAs remains challenging. Existing VLA post-training therefore often relies on simpler, readily scalable methods. One family directly updates the policy using high-quality experience, including filtered supervised fine-tuning ( Qin and Springenberg, 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , conditioned behavior cloning ( Intelligence et al., 2025a ) , and soft variants that weight demonstrations by estimated value ( Peng et al., 2019 ; Su et al., 2026 ) . A complementary family leaves the policy unchanged and instead uses learned value functions for test-time action selection, such as Best-of-N ( Nakamoto et al., 2024 ; Dodeja et al., 2026 ) , or by learning residual policies to modify the output action ( Ankile et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2026a ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) or steer the pre-trained policy’s denoising process ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) . We likewise focus on simple, scalable techniques, demonstrating (cf. Section 4 ) that they can achieve competitive performance. While these existing approaches to VLA post-training have demonstrated performance gains ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Ankile et al., 2025 ; Myers et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2026b ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Sun and Song, 2025 ) , they are limited, primarily, to improvement on single, individual tasks ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026b ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, we study joint post-training across increasingly broad task distributions and ask whether the resulting policy also improves on tasks outside the training distribution. Multi-task generalization. A separate literature studies how robotic performance scales with the diversity of training tasks. Prior work considers multi-task scaling without foundation-model policies ( Nauman et al., 2025 ) , while meta-reinforcement learning instead develops algorithms that learn to rapidly adapt to unseen tasks (rather than to directly transfer a fixed policy to new tasks, the setting we consider), traditionally with relatively small policies ( Duan et al., 2016 ; Finn et al., 2017 ; Yu et al., 2019 ) . More recent work extends this perspective to VLA policies through behavior cloning ( Bianchi et al., 2026 ) . Other works study generalization arising from scaling behavior cloning during pretraining ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Dyna Robotics, 2026 ) or post-training ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) . Here we focus on self-improvement via reinforcement learning. Perhaps closest to our setting is Liu et al. (2025) , who compare generalization of offline SFT from expert demonstrations with on-policy reinforcement-learning algorithms such as PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Our study differs in two important ways. First, Liu et al. (2025) utilize a single fixed distribution over training environments for all experiments; in contrast, a primary contribution of our work is quantifying which training distributions are necessary to induce generalization. Second, while we consider standard online RL fine-tuning procedures commonly used for VLAs, and study which such fine-tuning procedures enable generalization, this work compares non-RL approaches (SFT on expert demonstrations) to on-policy RL. While Liu et al. (2025) show that RL fine-tuning can enable greater generalization than SFT, our work provides informative guidance as to which design decisions are key to enabling this in practice. We note as well that multi-task generalization in post-training has been long studied in LLM post-training. We refer to Appendix A where we draw parallels to this work. 3 Problem Setting and Experimental Methodology 3.1 Problem Setting: Generalist Improvement of Generalist Policies We model our environment as a contextual Markov decision process ℳ = ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , 𝒞 , P , R , μ 0 , γ ) \mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{C},P,R,\mu_{0},\gamma) , where 𝒮 \mathcal{S} and 𝒜 \mathcal{A} are continuous state and action spaces, 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is a space of contexts encoding different tasks 1 1 1 In practice, a task will correspond to following a specific prompt in a specific manipulation environment. , P : 𝒮 × 𝒜 × 𝒞 → Δ ⁡ ( 𝒮 ) P:\mathcal{S\times A\times C}\to\Delta(\mathcal{S}) is a stochastic transition function, R : 𝒮 × 𝒜 × 𝒞 → [ R min , R max ] R:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{C}\to[R_{\min},R_{\max}] is a context-conditional reward function specifying each task, μ 0 : 𝒞 → Δ ⁡ ( 𝒮 ) \mu_{0}:\mathcal{C}\to\Delta(\mathcal{S}) is an initial distribution and γ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) \gamma\in[0,1) is a discount factor. items.raw_text: Reinforcement Learning Enables Scaling Generalist Robot Policy Improvement Michal Korniak Marco Bagatella Ralf Römer \BIGAND Michal Nauman Yarden As Pranav Vignesh Manan Agarwal Affiliation: ETH Zurich Affiliation: MPI for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen Affiliation: Technical University of Munich Affiliation: University of Warsaw Affiliation: Nomagic Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Leander Diaz-Bone Piotr Zalewski Mikołaj Czarnecki Affiliation: ETH Zurich Affiliation: MPI for Intelligent Systems, Tübingen Affiliation: University of Warsaw Affiliation: Nomagic Lenart Treven Shashwat Saxena Sreyas Venkataraman Affiliation: ETH Zurich Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Sarvesh Patil Zhiyuan Zhou Daniel Marta \BIGAND Oier Mees Nur Muhammad Mahi Shafiullah Carmelo Sferrazza Affiliation: ETH Zurich Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Affiliation: UC Berkeley Affiliation: Microsoft Bhavya Sukhija Angela P. Schoellig Andreas Krause \BIGAND Max Simchowitz Andrew Wagenmaker Affiliation: ETH Zurich Affiliation: Technical University of Munich Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University Affiliation: UC Berkeley Affiliation: Amazon FAR Affiliation: Physical Intelligence * Co-First Authors, order by coin flip † Co-Principal Investigators ‡ Lead Principal InvestigatorsProject page: https://lasgroup.github.io/generalist-improvement Repository: https://github.com/lasgroup/generalist-improvement Abstract The introduction of generalist robot policies has enabled a single, large model to learn to perform a variety of tasks from a vast pre-training corpus. While these models often exhibit powerful zero-shot generalization capabilities, they typically require an adaptation phase to achieve sufficient performance in deployment. Iterated self-improvement via reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated promise in enabling this adaptation, yet such approaches have been largely explored in single-task settings – where the goal is to simply improve on a narrow deployment task – which lies in stark contrast to the multi-task capabilities of the base policy. In this work we ask whether generalist robot policies are capable of multi-task, generalist improvement in deployment – targeting many diverse tasks simultaneously – and what algorithmic recipe enables this. To answer this question, we first develop a set of structured evaluations to test generalist improvement capabilities, and systematically evaluate algorithmic and practical design choices regarding value estimation, policy extraction and resource allocation. We show that not only can generalist policies be improved online across diverse tasks, but that the right recipe can enable generalization and increase performance on tasks not considered during online training. We characterize when this generalization occurs and show that both the training task distribution and the use of value-based RL are critical. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first evidence for online generalist improvement for robot foundation models. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Scaling the number of RL training tasks enables generalist improvement of generalist robot policies. As training task diversity increases, critic-guided policy extraction (OGPO) or refinement (BoN) prevent forgetting and improve performance on unseen tasks on MolmoSpaces , unlike filtered supervised fine-tuning (FSFT). Generalist robot policies, particularly Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs), have shown promise in enabling general-purpose robotic capabilities, allowing a single policy to be deployed across diverse tasks ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) . However, despite encoding diverse task-solving behaviors, such policies often lack sufficient reliability for robust deployment, and a degree of adaptation is typically necessary for effective performance ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2025b ; Reuss et al., 2025 ) . While enabling this adaptation through human supervision is often prohibitively expensive, autonomous adaptation through reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising approach to scale policy improvement, enabling robots to learn from their own experience in deployment ( Intelligence et al., 2025a ) . Yet, such autonomous improvement is typically limited to narrow single-task settings. As such, while these approaches enable generalist policies to improve, they may also specialize this improvement to the particular deployment task considered, and achieving improved performance on additional tasks of interest generally requires further online interaction and fine-tuning. A generalist policy, however, can produce a wide range of behaviors across diverse tasks, even if these behaviors may be far from optimal. Ideally we might hope that, by deploying on a diverse range of tasks, we could improve the performance of the policy across all tasks simultaneously – boosting its performance not just on a single deployment task, but on the entire distribution of tasks of interest. In particular, we might hope to enable truly generalist improvement : improvement on both the diverse set of tasks we deploy on, as well as generalization beyond these deployment tasks and improved performance on future novel deployment settings. This motivates the central question we consider in this work: how can we leverage interaction across a diverse set of tasks to enable online generalist improvement of generalist policies? That is, can a careful adaptation phase over multiple tasks enable both (i) improvement across these tasks simultaneously, and (ii) generalization beyond them, improving performance on tasks not encountered during post-training? In this paper, we undertake a systematic study to quantify generalist policy improvement across different axes of generalization. We show that appropriate recipes, when instantiated carefully, can enable not only generalist policy improvement across a diverse set of training tasks, but also task-generalization – improvement on tasks not seen during training. Further, we show that this improvement scales with the number and diversity of tasks trained on, as we showcase in Figure 1 . Our results suggest that moving beyond the single-task paradigm is not only possible but also crucial for achieving broader, generalist improvement. We isolate the essential algorithmic ingredients that enable multi-task learning and generalization. Specifically, we compare three families of learning approaches: (a) Direct Policy Adaptation , which directly improves the policy via filtered supervised fine-tuning on successful trajectories ( Peters and Schaal, 2007 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Qin and Springenberg, 2025 , FSFT,) . (b) Critic-Guided Test-Time Refinement , which uses test-time optimization against a learned state-action critic to improve actions. Here, we focus on Best-of-N sampling ( Nakamoto et al., 2024 ; Giridhar et al., 2026 , BoN,) with respect to that critic’s induced action ranking as a representative recipe. (c) Critic-Guided Policy Extraction , which updates a policy so as to maximize the value the critic assigns to the actions produced. Here, we adopt off-policy generative policy optimization ( Patil et al., 2026 , OGPO,) as a representative recipe, while also ablating alternative approaches such as combining FSFT and BoN sampling, or using AWR-inspired policy updates ( Peng et al., 2019 ) . Overall, while all three approaches enable some degree of generalization given a sufficient diversity in training tasks, we find that critic-guided methods enable a substantially greater degree of task generalization than direct policy adaptation alone . In particular, we show that critic-guided methods afford generalization both across training scenes, and, perhaps more surprisingly, across object types. Furthermore, we find that critic-guided policy extraction (OGPO) significantly outperforms test-time refinement (BoN), while also exhibiting similar scaling trends with training task diversity. This finding further points to critic-learning as the key component that enables generalist robotic policy improvement as task diversity scales. In addition to investigating algorithmic choices, we also systematically evaluate the training task distribution necessary for achieving such generalist improvement. We show that both the number of distinct training tasks, as well as the type of diversity exhibited in these training tasks, is critical to achieving generalist improvement. In particular, we find that a high degree of diversity in the required solution strategies within the training task distribution is crucial to learning generalizable task-solving behaviors. We believe these results illustrate a path forward for efficient online improvement of generalist robot policies. Rather than expensive single-task improvement on each deployment task of interest, our results show that, by amortizing this cost across a diverse set of tasks, one can enable generalist improvement, achieving improved performance on future deployment tasks of interest without paying the cost of additional online fine-tuning. 2 Related Work VLA post-training. Diffusion and flow-matching provide expressive generative policy classes that, when trained through behavior cloning at sufficient scale and diversity, can form the basis of generalist policies ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Reed et al., 2022 ) . Recent RL fine-tuning methods directly optimize such policies ( Psenka et al., 2024 ; Park et al., 2025b ; Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ; Patil et al., 2026 ; Li and Levine, 2026 ) , but scaling them to large VLAs remains challenging. Existing VLA post-training therefore often relies on simpler, readily scalable methods. One family directly updates the policy using high-quality experience, including filtered supervised fine-tuning ( Qin and Springenberg, 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , conditioned behavior cloning ( Intelligence et al., 2025a ) , and soft variants that weight demonstrations by estimated value ( Peng et al., 2019 ; Su et al., 2026 ) . A complementary family leaves the policy unchanged and instead uses learned value functions for test-time action selection, such as Best-of-N ( Nakamoto et al., 2024 ; Dodeja et al., 2026 ) , or by learning residual policies to modify the output action ( Ankile et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2026a ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) or steer the pre-trained policy’s denoising process ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) . We likewise focus on simple, scalable techniques, demonstrating (cf. Section 4 ) that they can achieve competitive performance. While these existing approaches to VLA post-training have demonstrated performance gains ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Ankile et al., 2025 ; Myers et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2026b ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Sun and Song, 2025 ) , they are limited, primarily, to improvement on single, individual tasks ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026b ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, we study joint post-training across increasingly broad task distributions and ask whether the resulting policy also improves on tasks outside the training distribution. Multi-task generalization. A separate literature studies how robotic performance scales with the diversity of training tasks. Prior work considers multi-task scaling without foundation-model policies ( Nauman et al., 2025 ) , while meta-reinforcement learning instead develops algorithms that learn to rapidly adapt to unseen tasks (rather than to directly transfer a fixed policy to new tasks, the setting we consider), traditionally with relatively small policies ( Duan et al., 2016 ; Finn et al., 2017 ; Yu et al., 2019 ) . More recent work extends this perspective to VLA policies through behavior cloning ( Bianchi et al., 2026 ) . Other works study generalization arising from scaling behavior cloning during pretraining ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Dyna Robotics, 2026 ) or post-training ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) . Here we focus on self-improvement via reinforcement learning. Perhaps closest to our setting is Liu et al. (2025) , who compare generalization of offline SFT from expert demonstrations with on-policy reinforcement-learning algorithms such as PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Our study differs in two important ways. First, Liu et al. (2025) utilize a single fixed distribution over training environments for all experiments; in contrast, a primary contribution of our work is quantifying which training distributions are necessary to induce generalization. Second, while we consider standard online RL fine-tuning procedures commonly used for VLAs, and study which such fine-tuning procedures enable generalization, this work compares non-RL approaches (SFT on expert demonstrations) to on-policy RL. While Liu et al. (2025) show that RL fine-tuning can enable greater generalization than SFT, our work provides informative guidance as to which design decisions are key to enabling this in practice. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.06879 (cs) [Submitted on 4 Nov 2026] Title: Adaptive Multi Mode: Budget-Aware Routing of Optimizers By Online Landscape Probes Authors: Benjamin Jacob Bodner View a PDF of the paper titled Adaptive Multi Mode: Budget-Aware Routing of Optimizers By Online Landscape Probes, by Benjamin Jacob Bodner View PDF Abstract: The best classical optimizer for a continuous black-box problem depends on its budget and landscape. Existing routers decide from the dimension and budget, past improvement or features fitted to one benchmark, and few test an optimizer's implicit assumptions online. AMM (Adaptive Multi Mode) routes a known budget among quasi-Newton, trust-region, coordinate, multistart and evolution-strategy optimization engines with online probes of curvature, plateaus, separability, kinks, basins and fractal structure. Each probe has a default, a dimension-by-budget validity range and a cost charged to the budget. In its pre-registered development loop on bbob, 32 of 36 predictions held over the last 16 confirmations. AMM was then tested once on held-out bbob instances 101-110 (D=2-40, 10*D-1000*D) against up to seven competitors. It has the highest target share in 382 of 600 function-dimension-budget cells (236 outright, 146 tied) and, by a descriptive posterior rule, is credibly behind in 35, mostly at 10*D and 30*D. At every budget it also leads the controls built from its own engines (the best engine alone, the best engine per dimension and budget, and a greedy schedule), narrowly at 10*D and 30*D, and nevergrad's NgIohTuned. In pre-registered runs its lead over IPOP-CMA-ES holds under affine and box transformations, on box-constrained bbob and, pooled, on rotated f2-f4, but rotating the separable f3 and f4 removes most of the lead there. On held-out MA-BBOB its final share at 2000*D is level with IPOP-CMA-ES's and its anytime area lower. We published AMM as an open-source Python package (pip install amm-optimizer; this https URL ). Comments: 29 pages, 8 figures, 19 tables. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.06846 (cs) [Submitted on 4 Nov 2026] Title: Navigating Disagreement Among Criteria for Evaluating Explanation Faithfulness Authors: Grant Shanklin , Jiří Němeček , Asia Biega View a PDF of the paper titled Navigating Disagreement Among Criteria for Evaluating Explanation Faithfulness, by Grant Shanklin and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Faithfulness requires that algorithmic explanations accurately reflect the model's behavior. Yet existing operationalizations of faithfulness can disagree about whether the same explanation is faithful, leaving developers and auditors to choose among conflicting evaluations. In this paper, we investigate disagreement among evaluation criteria and offer a practical path forward for evaluating explanation faithfulness. We first identify how operationalizations of faithfulness differ. We introduce a faithfulness functional that locates their disagreements in what an explanation claims about the model, which comparisons bear on that claim, and how agreement across those comparisons should be aggregated, and we reconstruct existing evaluation criteria within it. We argue these reconstructions support understanding faithfulness as a common though incompletely specified relation between the model and explanation, so the differences reflect choices left open by the general requirement. Justifying an operationalization then comes down to justifying these choices, which, on our view, draws on explanatory, institutional, and normative considerations. We support this argument with a case study of adverse action notices, reconstructing the evaluation implicit in an industry-proposed procedure and identifying which of its choices the setting justifies and which remain open. Our work gives auditors and practitioners a way to navigate disagreeing evaluations of faithfulness. It also explains why the literature should expect multiple operationalizations, while showing how concrete settings can narrow the choice among them. More broadly, our analysis shows how a shared requirement of faithfulness can support contextually justified evaluations despite disagreement among existing metrics.
