Faithfulness requires that algorithmic explanations accurately reflect the model’s behavior. Yet existing operationalizations of faithfulness can disagree about whether the same explanation is faithful, leaving developers and auditors to choose among conflicting evaluations. In this paper, we investigate disagreement among evaluation criteria and offer a practical path forward for evaluating explanation faithfulness. We first identify how operationalizations of faithfulness differ. We introduce a faithfulness functional that locates their disagreements in what an explanation claims about the model, which comparisons bear on that claim, and how agreement across those comparisons should be aggregated, and we reconstruct existing evaluation criteria within it. We argue these reconstructions support understanding faithfulness as a common though incompletely specified relation between the model and explanation, so the differences reflect choices left open by the general requirement. Justifying an operationalization then comes down to justifying these choices, which, on our view, draws on explanatory, institutional, and normative considerations. We support this argument with a case study of adverse action notices, reconstructing the evaluation implicit in an industry-proposed procedure and identifying which of its choices the setting justifies and which remain open. Our work gives auditors and practitioners a way to navigate disagreeing evaluations of faithfulness. It also explains why the literature should expect multiple operationalizations, while showing how concrete settings can narrow the choice among them. More broadly, our analysis shows how a shared requirement of faithfulness can support contextually justified evaluations despite disagreement among existing metrics. Keywords: explainability, faithfulness, evaluation, measurement, adverse action notices, consumer credit 1. Introduction Algorithmic explanations are commonly evaluated by breaking down desirable properties of explanations into distinct requirements and creating evaluations for each ( Nauta et al., 2023 ) . These requirements are derived from the purpose the explanation is meant to serve and the context in which it is used ( Lu et al., 2020 ) . One such requirement is faithfulness : the extent to which an explanation accurately represents the model’s behavior for a particular input ( Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020 ; Dasgupta et al., 2022 ) . Faithfulness is required for most use cases of explainability ( Krutský et al., 2025 ) , particularly when an explanation is used as evidence about why a model behaved as it did. For instance, faithfulness is required when a clinician uses an explanation to determine whether a model’s diagnosis rests on medically relevant evidence; an unfaithful explanation could therefore induce reliance on the wrong grounds ( Bussone et al., 2015 ) . Or a developer might use an explanation of an erroneous prediction to identify and correct the model’s reliance on a spurious feature; here, unfaithfulness could obscure the source of the error and misdirect the attempted correction ( Ribeiro et al., 2016 ; Adebayo et al., 2018 ) . The requirement of faithful explanations has further legal grounding. In the United States (US), when creditors take action against a consumer, such as denying a loan application, they are legally required to provide an explanation of why that action was taken in the form of an adverse action notice (AAN). AANs include the list of “principal reasons” the creditor acted against the consumer ( United States Congress, 1974 ; Fair Credit Reporting Act, 1970 ) . As black-box machine learning models have been introduced to these decision-making processes ( U.S. Department of the Treasury, 2024 ; Aldasoro et al., 2024 ) , algorithmic explanation methods have been proposed to generate such notices ( 3 ; Nair et al., 2024 ) . Both the regulatory text and the purposes of the underlying legislation require that the stated reasons accurately reflect the basis of the model’s decision, i.e., that the explanation be faithful ( FinRegLab, 2023 ; Selbst and Barocas, 2018 ) . Establishing that explanations ought to be faithful, however, does not yet tell us how to generate faithful explanations or determine whether a given explanation is faithful. Doing so requires operationalizing the general requirement, translating its natural-language definition into formal, mathematical terms, such that measurement and evaluation can be performed ( Jacobs and Wallach, 2021 ) . In our case, operationalizing faithfulness is what allows us to evaluate the extent to which an explanation is faithful to a model. The algorithmic explanation literature contains many operationalizations of faithfulness. This plurality is evident across methods for generating faithful explanations (e.g., ( Ribeiro et al., 2016 ; Ribeiro et al., 2018 ; Carter et al., 2019 ) ) and for evaluating the faithfulness of a given explanation (e.g., ( DeYoung et al., 2020 ; Dasgupta et al., 2022 ; Agarwal et al., 2022 ) ). However, these operationalizations substantially differ in what they require ( Krishna et al., 2024 ) ; a single explanation may be judged faithful under one and unfaithful under another ( Azzolin et al., 2025 ; Barr et al., 2023 ) . Multiple, non-equivalent operationalizations of faithfulness are problematic when we do not have a way to negotiate between them. Real-world implementations of faithful algorithmic explanations must choose among operationalizations, and so require a way to compare, evaluate, and select among different operationalizations of the same requirement. Existing work documents their disagreement ( Krishna et al., 2024 ; Barr et al., 2023 ) and unifies the explanation methods they evaluate ( Covert et al., 2021 ) , but does not say what would justify one operationalization over another for a given use. This has led to the sobering conclusion that some of these operationalizations “are not reliable enough to be used in real scenarios” ( Miró-Nicolau et al., 2025 ) and that, at least in settings with graph neural networks, faithfulness may not be “a sensible design goal” ( Azzolin et al., 2025 ) . The task of our paper is to provide a framework for justifying choices among non-equivalent operationalizations of faithfulness. We make explicit the substantive, and often contextual, choices that enter an evaluation and examine what can justify them. This allows us to distinguish choices supported by an explanation’s setting from those that are not. Our contribution helps explain why conflicting evaluations exist within the literature and gives auditors and practitioners a way to assess their suitability for a particular use. More broadly, this work bears on the theoretical foundations of algorithmic explanation, which have been criticized as under-theorized ( Moshkovitz et al., 2026 ; Watson, 2022 ; Afroogh et al., 2026 ) . We follow recent work ( Jacobs and Wallach, 2021 ; Coston et al., 2023 ; Wallach et al., 2024 ) that develops these foundations through measurement modeling. 1.1. Contributions This work is structured around the idea that understanding how faithfulness evaluations in the literature differ will help explain why they differ. Clarifying points of disagreement between operationalizations guides what matters when choosing among them. We thus make our contribution in three parts. First, we introduce a common representation of faithfulness operationalizations for two classes of local explanation methods (Section 3 ) . We propose a three-component functional representation that writes each operationalization in the same formal terms. We show that a varied set of faithfulness operationalizations can be reconstructed within the functional framework, differing only in what we call the faithfulness specification . Under this reconstruction, each operationalization tests whether the model’s behavior accords with the claim attributed to the explanation. Second, we use the reconstructions to argue that faithfulness names a common but incompletely specified relation between an explanation and model behavior (Section 4 ) . The reconstructed criteria differ in substantive choices that remain open even when faithfulness is understood as accurately representing model behavior. We distinguish these specification choices from disagreements about the underlying concept and errors in measuring a fixed target. This interpretation explains how multiple operationalizations can express a shared requirement while yielding different evaluations. Finally, we identify explanatory, institutional, and normative considerations that bear on the justification of a faithfulness specification (Section 5 ) . We apply this framework to adverse action notices, reconstructing the evaluation implicit in a US bank’s proposed reason-selection procedure, which ranks fixed-length notices by their mean B-Shap contribution. We then examine which choices receive support from the disclosure setting and which remain unresolved. The case shows how the framework can make an evaluation’s commitments explicit and subject them to contextual scrutiny. 1.2. Related Work Existing work has sought to clarify the differences between algorithmic explanation methods by representing them in common formal terms. These representations identify choices about how features are removed and their influence summarized ( Covert et al., 2021 ) , which neighborhood is used to approximate the model ( Han et al., 2022 ) , and which reference distribution is used to compute an attribution ( Merrick and Taly, 2020 ) . Related work on evaluation shows that the choice of operationalization can affect whether an explanation is judged faithful. For instance, Azzolin et al. (2025) parameterize faithfulness metrics for graph neural networks and recommend choosing parameters according to the task. Faithfulness requires that algorithmic explanations accurately reflect the model’s behavior. Yet existing operationalizations of faithfulness can disagree about whether the same explanation is faithful, leaving developers and auditors to choose among conflicting evaluations. In this paper, we investigate disagreement among evaluation criteria and offer a practical path forward for evaluating explanation faithfulness. We first identify how operationalizations of faithfulness differ. We introduce a faithfulness functional that locates their disagreements in what an explanation claims about the model, which comparisons bear on that claim, and how agreement across those comparisons should be aggregated, and we reconstruct existing evaluation criteria within it. We argue these reconstructions support understanding faithfulness as a common though incompletely specified relation between the model and explanation, so the differences reflect choices left open by the general requirement. Justifying an operationalization then comes down to justifying these choices, which, on our view, draws on explanatory, institutional, and normative considerations. We support this argument with a case study of adverse action notices, reconstructing the evaluation implicit in an industry-proposed procedure and identifying which of its choices the setting justifies and which remain open. Our work gives auditors and practitioners a way to navigate disagreeing evaluations of faithfulness. It also explains why the literature should expect multiple operationalizations, while showing how concrete settings can narrow the choice among them. More broadly, our analysis shows how a shared requirement of faithfulness can support contextually justified evaluations despite disagreement among existing metrics. Introduction Algorithmic explanations are commonly evaluated by breaking down desirable properties of explanations into distinct requirements and creating evaluations for each ( Nauta et al., 2023 ) . These requirements are derived from the purpose the explanation is meant to serve and the context in which it is used ( Lu et al., 2020 ) . One such requirement is faithfulness : the extent to which an explanation accurately represents the model’s behavior for a particular input ( Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020 ; Dasgupta et al., 2022 ) . Faithfulness is required for most use cases of explainability ( Krutský et al., 2025 ) , particularly when an explanation is used as evidence about why a model behaved as it did. For instance, faithfulness is required when a clinician uses an explanation to determine whether a model’s diagnosis rests on medically relevant evidence; an unfaithful explanation could therefore induce reliance on the wrong grounds ( Bussone et al., 2015 ) . Or a developer might use an explanation of an erroneous prediction to identify and correct the model’s reliance on a spurious feature; here, unfaithfulness could obscure the source of the error and misdirect the attempted correction ( Ribeiro et al., 2016 ; Adebayo et al., 2018 ) . The requirement of faithful explanations has further legal grounding. In the United States (US), when creditors take action against a consumer, such as denying a loan application, they are legally required to provide an explanation of why that action was taken in the form of an adverse action notice (AAN). AANs include the list of “principal reasons” the creditor acted against the consumer ( United States Congress, 1974 ; Fair Credit Reporting Act, 1970 ) . As black-box machine learning models have been introduced to these decision-making processes ( U.S. Department of the Treasury, 2024 ; Aldasoro et al., 2024 ) , algorithmic explanation methods have been proposed to generate such notices ( 3 ; Nair et al., 2024 ) . Both the regulatory text and the purposes of the underlying legislation require that the stated reasons accurately reflect the basis of the model’s decision, i.e., that the explanation be faithful ( FinRegLab, 2023 ; Selbst and Barocas, 2018 ) . Establishing that explanations ought to be faithful, however, does not yet tell us how to generate faithful explanations or determine whether a given explanation is faithful. Doing so requires operationalizing the general requirement, translating its natural-language definition into formal, mathematical terms, such that measurement and evaluation can be performed ( Jacobs and Wallach, 2021 ) . In our case, operationalizing faithfulness is what allows us to evaluate the extent to which an explanation is faithful to a model. The algorithmic explanation literature contains many operationalizations of faithfulness. This plurality is evident across methods for generating faithful explanations (e.g., ( Ribeiro et al., 2016 ; Ribeiro et al., 2018 ; Carter et al., 2019 ) ) and for evaluating the faithfulness of a given explanation (e.g., ( DeYoung et al., 2020 ; Dasgupta et al., 2022 ; Agarwal et al., 2022 ) ). However, these operationalizations substantially differ in what they require ( Krishna et al., 2024 ) ; a single explanation may be judged faithful under one and unfaithful under another ( Azzolin et al., 2025 ; Barr et al., 2023 ) . Multiple, non-equivalent operationalizations of faithfulness are problematic when we do not have a way to negotiate between them. Real-world implementations of faithful algorithmic explanations must choose among operationalizations, and so require a way to compare, evaluate, and select among different operationalizations of the same requirement. Existing work documents their disagreement ( Krishna et al., 2024 ; Barr et al., 2023 ) and unifies the explanation methods they evaluate ( Covert et al., 2021 ) , but does not say what would justify one operationalization over another for a given use. This has led to the sobering conclusion that some of these operationalizations “are not reliable enough to be used in real scenarios” ( Miró-Nicolau et al., 2025 ) and that, at least in settings with graph neural networks, faithfulness may not be “a sensible design goal” ( Azzolin et al., 2025 ) . The task of our paper is to provide a framework for justifying choices among non-equivalent operationalizations of faithfulness. We make explicit the substantive, and often contextual, choices that enter an evaluation and examine what can justify them. This allows us to distinguish choices supported by an explanation’s setting from those that are not. Our contribution helps explain why conflicting evaluations exist within the literature and gives auditors and practitioners a way to assess their suitability for a particular use. More broadly, this work bears on the theoretical foundations of algorithmic explanation, which have been criticized as under-theorized ( Moshkovitz et al., 2026 ; Watson, 2022 ; Afroogh et al., 2026 ) . We follow recent work ( Jacobs and Wallach, 2021 ; Coston et al., 2023 ; Wallach et al., 2024 ) that develops these foundations through measurement modeling. 1.1. We propose a three-component functional representation that writes each operationalization in the same formal terms. We show that a varied set of faithfulness operationalizations can be reconstructed within the functional framework, differing only in what we call the faithfulness specification . items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.06837 (cs) [Submitted on 4 Nov 2026] Title: Context--Answer Metamodels: Forecasting LLM Activations Before the First Answer Token Authors: Tommy He , Thomas Jiralerspong View a PDF of the paper titled Context--Answer Metamodels: Forecasting LLM Activations Before the First Answer Token, by Tommy He and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Under stochastic decoding, a single context can elicit many different answers from a language model. Characterizing this variation typically requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization. We ask whether the activations produced while reading the context can directly forecast the model's rollout activations. We train context--answer metamodels that map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations. We find that (i) the four metamodel families we study forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; (ii) performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts, and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets; (iii) their forecasts retain behavior-predictive signal; and (iv) context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, suggesting that activation forecasts can transfer across models. Together, these results suggest that context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of behaviors in LLM answers before the first answer token is generated. items.content: \setmathfont latinmodern-math.otf[range=”22A4] \tufasetup title=Context–Answer Metamodels: Forecasting LLM Activations Before the First Answer Token, short-title=Context–Answer Metamodels, authors=Tommy He 1 Thomas Jiralerspong 2 , pdf-authors=Tommy He and Thomas Jiralerspong, affiliation= 1 Tufa Labs 2 Mila, Université de Montréal, date=4 November 2026, contact=tommy@tufalabs.ai, code-url=https://github.com/Tufalabs/context-answer-metamodels, Abstract Under stochastic decoding, a single context can elicit many different answers from a language model. Characterizing this variation typically requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization. We ask whether the activations produced while reading the context can directly forecast the model’s rollout activations. We train context–answer metamodels that map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations. We find that (i) the four metamodel families we study forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; (ii) performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts, and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets; (iii) their forecasts retain behavior-predictive signal; and (iv) context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, suggesting that activation forecasts can transfer across models. Together, these results suggest that context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of behaviors in LLM answers before the first answer token is generated. 1 Introduction How much of a language model’s future output is predictable before it emits its first answer token? Under stochastic decoding, a single context can produce different answer trajectories even when the model and decoding configuration are held fixed. Estimating this variability normally requires sampling multiple expensive rollouts. We ask whether we can forecast it directly from context activations. Such a forecast is useful in applications where a single completion is an unreliable indicator of a model’s possible behavior, such as pre-generation rare-behavior screening and pass@ k k estimation. Behavior screening often samples many answers and scores them with a probe or another language model. This is costly for rare events, and it provides no warning before the sampled behavior occurs. Rather than modeling combinatorially many complete token sequences directly, we forecast their answer representations. Prior work predicts later tokens and hidden states from earlier activations [ Pal et al., 2023 ] , while other work uses context activations to predict answer attributes, hallucination risk, and answer correctness [ Dong et al., 2025 , Ji et al., 2024 , Moreno Cencerrado et al., 2025 ] . Most closely related, Jiralerspong et al. [2026] fit linear and nonlinear context–answer maps on 500,000 training prompts, with one sampled answer per prompt. We study point and distribution forecasts under repeated-rollout supervision and evaluate both. We train context–answer metamodels 1 1 1 Code repository: https://github.com/Tufalabs/context-answer-metamodels . on context activation traces and repeated answer activation traces from rollouts of a language model. Point metamodels forecast the expectation of the mean-pooled answer activation; distribution metamodels forecast its rollout-induced distribution. Figure 1 summarizes the training and evaluation procedure. We additionally test whether the forecasts preserve behavior-predictive directions present in real answer activations. Our contributions are: • We compare linear ridge and MLP predictors of the conditional mean with Gaussian and flow models of rollout variability. • We show continued scaling through 500,000 training prompts and zero-shot out-of-domain transfer from LMSYS to WeirdChat and IFEval. • We show that forecasted answer activations retain behavior-predictive signal. • We show that context activations from Qwen2.5 can forecast Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4 answer activations, retaining most of the accuracy of matched target-model conditioners at scale. The metamodel receives context activations from a language model and produces either a point forecast of the expected mean-pooled answer activation (linear ridge or MLP) or a distribution forecast over mean-pooled answer activations (Gaussian or flow). Multiple decoding seeds provide training and evaluation targets. 2 Methodology 2.1 Problem formulation Let M M be a frozen autoregressive language model with hidden dimension d d , D D a fixed stochastic decoding configuration, and x x an input context (prompt) with token length T x T_{x} . Let s ∼ ℙ D s\sim\mathbb{P}_{D} denote a pseudorandom seed. Prefill at the output of decoder block ℓ \ell yields a context activation trace C ℓ ​ ( x ) ∈ ℝ T x × d C_{\ell}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{x}\times d} . A rollout under D D yields a variable-length answer activation trace that we mean-pool into A ℓ ​ ( x , s ) ∈ ℝ d A_{\ell}(x,s)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} [ Wang et al., 2026 , Der et al., 2026 ] . This stochastic decoding process defines both a conditional expectation and a conditional law: μ ℓ ​ ( x ) \displaystyle\mu_{\ell}(x) : = 𝔼 s ∼ ℙ D ​ [ A ℓ ​ ( x , s ) ∣ x ] \displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathbb{P}_{D}}\!\left[A_{\ell}(x,s)\mid x\right] (1) P ℓ x \displaystyle P_{\ell}^{x} : = Law M , D ⁡ ( A ℓ ​ ( x , s ) ∣ x ) . \displaystyle:=\operatorname{Law}_{M,D}\!\left(A_{\ell}(x,s)\mid x\right). We accordingly study two prediction targets: a point metamodel models the expectation μ ℓ \mu_{\ell} , and a distribution metamodel models the whole rollout-induced law, P ℓ x P_{\ell}^{x} . We write μ ^ ℓ ​ ( x ) \widehat{\mu}_{\ell}(x) and P ^ ℓ x \widehat{P}_{\ell}^{x} for the corresponding learned forecasts, appending a model-family subscript only when needed. 2.2 Four metamodel families We train two point metamodels (linear ridge and MLP) and two distribution metamodels (Gaussian and flow). We select the former by validation R 2 R^{2} and the latter by validation energy score. For inputs, the linear ridge model takes the final context-token activation, whereas the MLP and flow take a 32-bin context trace (the Gaussian extends a frozen MLP). Adaptive average pooling forms B = 32 B=32 contiguous, approximately equal-sized bins that may overlap, reusing tokens when T x < 32 T_{x}<32 . We pool the bin averages r 1 , … , r B ∈ ℝ d r_{1},\ldots,r_{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with a learned query q q : α j = softmax j ⁡ ( q ⊤ ​ LN ⁡ ( r j ) d ) , z = ∑ j = 1 B α j ​ r j . \alpha_{j}=\operatorname{softmax}_{j}\left(\frac{q^{\top}\operatorname{LN}(r_{j})}{\sqrt{d}}\right),\qquad z=\sum_{j=1}^{B}\alpha_{j}r_{j}. (2) We use single-query, query-only attention pooling: q q is one learned global query, the normalized bins directly compute its attention scores, and the unprojected bins are the values. This pooling is the first learned stage: z z is passed directly to the downstream MLP or flow, and q q is trained jointly with it. Linear ridge point metamodel. The linear ridge forecast is μ ^ ℓ , lin ​ ( x ) = W ​ h ~ last + b \widehat{\mu}_{\ell,\mathrm{lin}}(x)=W\widetilde{h}_{\mathrm{last}}+b , where h ~ last \widetilde{h}_{\mathrm{last}} is the final context-token activation, coordinatewise standardized using training statistics. We fit this full-dimensional map to empirical rollout means in closed form, selecting the ridge penalty λ \lambda by validation R 2 R^{2} . Appendix Figure 5 ablates the choice of input representation. MLP point metamodel. The MLP forecast μ ^ ℓ , MLP ​ ( x ) \widehat{\mu}_{\ell,\mathrm{MLP}}(x) maps z z through a three-layer 4,096 → 8,192 → 8,192 → 4,096 4{,}096{\rightarrow}\allowbreak 8{,}192{\rightarrow}\allowbreak 8{,}192{\rightarrow}\allowbreak 4{,}096 GELU MLP (134.2M parameters) and minimizes MSE against each prompt’s empirical mean over training rollouts. We estimate Σ \Sigma from within-prompt residuals A ℓ ​ ( x , s ) − A ¯ ℓ ​ ( x ) A_{\ell}(x,s)-\overline{A}_{\ell}(x) , where A ¯ ℓ ​ ( x ) \overline{A}_{\ell}(x) is the empirical rollout mean. Candidate covariances are isotropic, diagonal, or low-rank-plus-diagonal. The scale is global ( γ ⁡ ( z ) = 1 \gamma(z)=1 ) or prompt-dependent. For the latter, γ ⁡ ( z ) \gamma(z) is a normalized scale derived from a two-layer 4,096 → 256 → 1 4{,}096{\rightarrow}256{\rightarrow}1 SiLU head’s log-variance prediction (Appendix D ). Covariance family, rank, scale mode, and the scalar multiplier κ \kappa are selected by validation energy score. Flow distribution metamodel. We use conditional flow matching with a linear path [ Lipman et al., 2023 ] . Integrating v θ ​ ( y t , t , z ) v_{\theta}(y_{t},t,z) from a Gaussian base draw ε \varepsilon at t = 0 t=0 to t = 1 t=1 produces a sample A ~ ℓ ∼ P ^ ℓ , F x \widetilde{A}_{\ell}\sim\widehat{P}_{\ell,\mathrm{F}}^{x} . For each rollout target y y , base draw ε \varepsilon , and t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1] , we set y t = ( 1 − t ) ​ ε + t ​ y y_{t}=(1-t)\varepsilon+ty and minimize ℒ FM ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ‖ v θ ​ ( y t , t , z ) − ( y − ε ) ‖ 2 2 ] . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|v_{\theta}(y_{t},t,z)-(y-\varepsilon)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]. (3) The vector field v θ v_{\theta} has width 4,096, sinusoidal time embeddings, and eight conditioned residual blocks (352.8M parameters). At inference, 64 Gaussian base draws are integrated for 32 Euler steps. We select the final model with the lowest validation energy score. Appendix Figure 7 ablates the choice of input representation. 2.3 Experimental setup Our primary study uses decoder block 18 of Qwen3.5-9B [ Qwen Team, 2026 ] , selected in Appendix Figure 9 . All layer indices are zero-indexed and refer to raw decoder-block outputs. LMSYS-Chat-1M [ Zheng et al., 2024 ] provides 500,000/1,000/3,000 train/validation/test prompts, each with four independently seeded rollouts. The rollout-count ablation uses 100,000 training prompts, the same validation/test sizes, and a common 16-rollout evaluation target. Out-of-domain (OOD) evaluation uses all 2,660 WeirdChat prompts [ Chowdhury et al., 2026 ] and 541 IFEval prompts [ Zhou et al., 2023 ] , with frozen LMSYS metamodels and four observed rollouts per prompt. We evaluate the linear ridge and MLP forecasts and the flow mean using pooled multivariate R 2 R^{2} against the empirical rollout mean (“mean R 2 R^{2} ”). The Gaussian’s analytic mean equals the MLP forecast. For the Gaussian and flow, we add the energy score [ Gneiting and Raftery, 2007 ] divided by d \sqrt{d} , Spearman correlation between predicted and observed prompt-level variance, and the ratio of generated to observed variance (definitions and secondary metrics in Appendix C ). For cross-model forecasting, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct layer 19 context activations [ Yang et al., 2024 ] predict Qwen3.5-9B layer 18 and Gemma-4-12B-it layer 47 answer activations [ Google DeepMind, 2026 ] , with matched target-model conditioners as controls. Layers 19 and 47 are fixed from earlier validation-selected final context-token activation sweeps (Appendix G ). Appendix D gives the full experimental settings. 3 Results 3.1 Context activation traces forecast answer activations at scale and generalize OOD Figure 2 shows a clear scale-dependent reversal in mean R 2 R^{2} . The linear ridge metamodel initially outperforms the nonlinear MLP and flow mean on all three evaluation sets, but the nonlinear models overtake it as prompt coverage grows. The linear ridge curves then plateau much earlier. At the largest scale, the flow mean approaches the MLP on both OOD sets, with a modest gap in domain. The full context trace further improves both neural models (Appendix A ). Table 1 reports endpoint distribution metrics: the Gaussian has a slightly better LMSYS energy score and variance ranking, whereas the flow has lower OOD energy scores. Appendix Figure 11 shows the corresponding scaling curves, and Appendix Figure 10 reports prompt retrieval. Appendix F visualizes the forecasts. Increasing prompt coverage is more valuable than adding repeated targets: eight rollouts capture most of the gain from sixteen (Appendix Figure 8 ). Figure 2 : Prompt coverage drives forecast quality through the largest tested scale, in and out of domain. Columns correspond to evaluation sets and show mean R 2 R^{2} for the linear ridge, MLP, and flow metamodels. All metamodels are trained only on LMSYS; WeirdChat (2,660 prompts) and IFEval (541 prompts) are zero-shot, with four rollouts per prompt. The linear ridge metamodel uses the final context-token activation and the neural models use the 32-bin context trace. Other endpoint metrics are in Table 1 . This analysis uses new metamodel fits on both LMSYS and the WeirdChat training split. The direct-context baseline predicts behavior from context activations without an answer forecast; each context-only score is assigned to all four answers for answer-level evaluation (Appendix H ). Figure 3 shows answer-level AUPRC on held-out WeirdChat prompts, with labels from GPT-6 Luna [ OpenAI, 2026 ] . Pre-generation probes predict answer structure and content [ Dong et al., 2025 ] , hallucination risk [ Ji et al., 2024 ] , and answer correctness [ Moreno Cencerrado et al., 2025 ] . The Tuned Lens decodes intermediate-layer next-token predictions [ Belrose et al., 2023 ] ; Future Lens predicts later tokens and hidden states [ Pal et al., 2023 ] ; and EAGLE predicts near-future features for speculative decoding [ Li et al., 2024 ] . Characterizing this variation typically requires many expensive autoregressive rollouts, each revealing only one realization. We ask whether the activations produced while reading the context can directly forecast the model’s rollout activations. We train context–answer metamodels that map a context activation sequence to point or distribution forecasts of mean-pooled answer activations. We find that (i) the four metamodel families we study forecast mean-pooled answer activations with high fidelity, and the distribution metamodels also capture rollout variability; (ii) performance improves as the training set grows to 500,000 prompts, and the metamodels generalize zero-shot to out-of-domain datasets; (iii) their forecasts retain behavior-predictive signal; and (iv) context activations from Qwen2.5 predict mean-pooled answer activations from Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4, suggesting that activation forecasts can transfer across models. Together, these results suggest that context activation traces can support scalable forecasts of behaviors in LLM answers before the first answer token is generated. 1 Introduction How much of a language model’s future output is predictable before it emits its first answer token? Under stochastic decoding, a single context can produce different answer trajectories even when the model and decoding configuration are held fixed. Estimating this variability normally requires sampling multiple expensive rollouts. We ask whether we can forecast it directly from context activations. Such a forecast is useful in applications where a single completion is an unreliable indicator of a model’s possible behavior, such as pre-generation rare-behavior screening and pass@ k k estimation. Behavior screening often samples many answers and scores them with a probe or another language model. This is costly for rare events, and it provides no warning before the sampled behavior occurs. Rather than modeling combinatorially many complete token sequences directly, we forecast their answer representations. Prior work predicts later tokens and hidden states from earlier activations [ Pal et al., 2023 ] , while other work uses context activations to predict answer attributes, hallucination risk, and answer correctness [ Dong et al., 2025 , Ji et al., 2024 , Moreno Cencerrado et al., 2025 ] . Most closely related, Jiralerspong et al. [2026] fit linear and nonlinear context–answer maps on 500,000 training prompts, with one sampled answer per prompt. We study point and distribution forecasts under repeated-rollout supervision and evaluate both. We train context–answer metamodels 1 1 1 Code repository: https://github.com/Tufalabs/context-answer-metamodels . on context activation traces and repeated answer activation traces from rollouts of a language model. Point metamodels forecast the expectation of the mean-pooled answer activation; distribution metamodels forecast its rollout-induced distribution. Figure 1 summarizes the training and evaluation procedure. We additionally test whether the forecasts preserve behavior-predictive directions present in real answer activations. Our contributions are: • We compare linear ridge and MLP predictors of the conditional mean with Gaussian and flow models of rollout variability. • We show continued scaling through 500,000 training prompts and zero-shot out-of-domain transfer from LMSYS to WeirdChat and IFEval. • We show that forecasted answer activations retain behavior-predictive signal. • We show that context activations from Qwen2.5 can forecast Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4 answer activations, retaining most of the accuracy of matched target-model conditioners at scale. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2611.06828 (cs) [Submitted on 4 Nov 2026] Title: Systolic Linear Attention: Co-Designing Tile-Grouped Gated Delta Attention for TPUs Authors: Gagik Amirkhanyan , Nuojin Cheng View a PDF of the paper titled Systolic Linear Attention: Co-Designing Tile-Grouped Gated Delta Attention for TPUs, by Gagik Amirkhanyan and Nuojin Cheng View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Gated-delta linear attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), and GDN-2 are tuned for GPUs, where small tensor-core tiles and fast vector registers make per-channel decay rescaling and sequential in-block solves cheap. On Google TPUs, which concentrate compute in wide $256 \times 256$ systolic matrix units backed by a slower vector unit, porting these layers directly leaves half of each matrix tile empty and bottlenecks on vector operations. We present \textbf{Systolic Linear Attention (SLA)}, which reshapes gated delta attention around the matrix unit by widening keys to $256$ with grouped value heads, grouping decay gates into four $64$-channel tiles, and computing the chunk solve entirely with block matrix products in a single fused kernel. On TPU v7x, a full \texttt{SLA-R4} layer runs $1.6\times$--$2.5\times$ faster than the open-source Tokamax KDA kernel ($1.4\times$--$2.4\times$ with exact chunk inversion), driven primarily by head sharing and kernel fusion. Across a $2{,}048$-chip TPU v7x pre-training study of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models from $6.5\text{B}$ to $63.1\text{B}$ parameters, SLA trains $11\%$--$24\%$ faster than KDA at similar perplexity, and reaches slightly lower perplexity than KDA in smaller matched-seed runs. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER, a Benchmark for evaluating Embodied Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs. items.content: BEAKER BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories Xue Yang Abstract Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are moving chemical experimentation toward embodied automation, where machines must perceive laboratory scenes, reason about experimental states, and act under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Although Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly considered as embodied brains for such systems, existing laboratory benchmarks mainly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific understanding, leaving their execution-oriented embodied capabilities underexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER , a B enchmark for evaluating E mbodied A ctionability, K nowledge, E xperimentation, and R easoning in SDCLs. BEAKER contains 1,000 expert-curated question-answer samples across 11 image and video task types, covering key judgments required for chemical laboratory execution, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, equipment, state, and safety recognition, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. All questions and annotations are manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts, without AI-assisted generation or annotation. We evaluate 28 general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied MLLMs in an offline, single-turn setting. Results show that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures in videos, but still struggle to ground actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to recognize fine-grained laboratory apparatus, states, and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures. BEAKER thus reveals a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception required for laboratory execution, providing a diagnostic benchmark for future MLLMs in SDCLs. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Overview of BEAKER and key evaluation findings. The radar chart compares four representative models across 11 tasks grouped by capability. All axes use a 0–100 scale except AFF, which uses a 0–50 scale due to uniformly low scores across all models. AFF: Affordance Grounding; TRAJ: Trajectory Planning; ERI: Equipment and Reagent Identification; ESS: Experimental Safety and Standardization; SR: State Recognition; EAS: Experimental Apparatus Setup; EOP: Experimental Operations; SVOR: Short-Video Operation Reasoning; MVTS: Mid-Video Task-Step Reasoning; TSR: Temporal Sequence Reasoning; LVPR: Long-Video Experimental Procedure Reasoning; GT: Ground Truth. Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories (SDCLs) are transforming chemical experimentation from manual trial-and-error into closed-loop autonomous discovery, where automated devices execute experiments, observe outcomes, and use data-driven feedback to guide subsequent operations [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Such systems require more than predefined protocol execution: automated devices must perceive laboratory scenes, understand experimental states, and make execution-relevant judgments under physical, procedural, and safety constraints. Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serving as embodied brains provide a promising paradigm for this goal, aiming to connect multimodal perception with affordance reasoning, task progress, physical constraints, and action-oriented decision-making [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . However, existing embodied brain studies mainly focus on general robotic and embodied scenarios, while scientific experimental automation remains much less explored. This requirement is non-trivial because chemical experiments are not static visual scenes but procedural, operable, and safety-constrained embodied processes, in which visual information becomes meaningful only in the context of the current execution. The same apparatus, liquid level, connection state, or material change may imply different actions, risks, or experimental outcomes depending on the current step, operability, connection correctness, and safety requirements. Recognizing a flask, a liquid interface, or a connected tube is therefore insufficient if a model cannot determine whether the apparatus is ready to operate, whether the connection supports the next step, or whether an observed state change indicates normal progress or potential failure. This raises a central question: can current MLLMs move from laboratory scene understanding to execution-grounded reasoning in chemical experiments? Recent studies have begun to explore MLLMs in SDCLs, demonstrating their potential in robotic chemical operations, experimental state monitoring, and safety risk identification [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] . Meanwhile, emerging laboratory-oriented multimodal benchmarks mainly focus on anomaly detection, hazard identification, safety planning, or general scientific understanding [ 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ] . While valuable, they do not systematically assess the embodied capabilities required for automated experimental execution. A suitable benchmark for SDCL-oriented embodied brains should evaluate whether MLLMs can identify operable regions, understand laboratory apparatus and states, track execution steps, and reason about temporal changes and experimental outcomes. To fill this gap, we introduce BEAKER , short for B enchmark for E mbodied A ctionability, K nowledge, E xperimentation, and R easoning in SDCLs (Fig. 1 ). BEAKER decomposes embodied chemical laboratory execution into four core capabilities, each evaluated through expert-designed Question-Answering (QA) tasks. Actionability concerns whether a model understands operable regions, interaction possibilities, and motion feasibility. Knowledge concerns whether it recognizes laboratory apparatus, experimental states, and procedural norms. Experimentation concerns whether it understands experimental operations, apparatus connections, and step progression. Reasoning concerns whether it can infer temporal changes, procedural consequences, and experimental outcomes. Together, these dimensions provide an execution-oriented framework for evaluating whether MLLMs can support automated chemical experimentation beyond passive scene understanding. Specifically, we collect more than 10,000 publicly available real-world images and videos related to chemical laboratories. Most samples are collected from first-person or experiment-execution-related viewpoints, covering diverse chemical laboratory scenes and workbenches. All samples are jointly selected, reviewed, and annotated by chemistry experts and embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) experts. The resulting BEAKER dataset contains 1,000 carefully designed QA samples, covering seven image-based task types and four video-based task types. All questions are manually authored by human experts according to chemical laboratory execution contexts, without using AI tools for sample selection, question generation, or annotation, thereby reducing the self-bias that may arise from the MLLM-as-benchmark-generator paradigm. These tasks do not merely test chemical commonsense or laboratory object recognition; instead, they evaluate, in an offline, single-turn setting, the execution-grounded perception and reasoning on which closed-loop SDCL execution depends. We further evaluate 28 mainstream MLLMs on BEAKER, including general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized, and embodied multimodal models. The results reveal that current models can follow coarse procedural progress in experimental videos, but still struggle with execution-oriented judgments. In particular, localizing fine-grained operable regions, planning feasible trajectories, recognizing domain-specific apparatus, reagent states, and safety norms, and ordering steps in mid-length procedures remain challenging, while science-oriented and chemistry-specialized models do not consistently outperform general-purpose MLLMs. These findings reveal that domain knowledge alone is insufficient for SDCL execution and that current models still need to ground laboratory observations into operable actions, procedural progress, and experimental outcomes. In summary, our contributions are as follows: • We introduce BEAKER , an offline, single-turn benchmark for evaluating multimodal embodied brains in SDCLs, which organizes chemical laboratory automation capabilities into four core dimensions: Actionability , Knowledge , Experimentation , and Reasoning . • We construct a multimodal dataset with 1,000 QA samples across 11 key tasks. All samples are manually selected and annotated by domain experts to ensure that the evaluation remains grounded in realistic chemical laboratory execution contexts. • We evaluate 28 mainstream MLLMs on BEAKER and reveal a clear execution gap: current models can follow coarse experimental procedures, but still struggle with fine-grained action grounding, domain-specific laboratory perception, and mid-length procedural reasoning for SDCL automation. 2 Related Work 2.1 MLLM-enabled SDCL General-purpose MLLMs have shown strong abilities in image understanding, video reasoning, and long-context modeling [ 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 , 36 , 37 ] . Science-oriented MLLMs further incorporate domain-specific scientific data and reasoning tasks [ 38 , 39 ] , while chemistry-specialized MLLMs target molecular structures, reaction images, and cross-modal chemical knowledge [ 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 ] . In parallel, embodied MLLMs extend vision-language reasoning to physical-action scenarios, such as spatial understanding, affordance detection, trajectory prediction, and task planning [ 15 , 44 , 45 , 46 ] . These advances make MLLMs potential embodied brains for SDCLs. Recent works have applied MLLMs to robotic chemical operations [ 19 , 47 ] , execution-state monitoring with visual inspection and error correction [ 18 ] , and human-aware laboratory coordination [ 48 ] . However, real chemical experiments are dynamic, transparent, step-dependent, and safety-constrained, making visual grounding, state judgment, and error recovery still challenging. 2.2 Multimodal Embodied Brains and QA Benchmarks Multimodal embodied brains [ 10 , 15 , 49 , 46 , 45 , 50 , 13 , 51 , 52 , 53 , 54 , 16 , 55 ] are high-level cognitive models for physical-action scenarios, integrating vision, language, and task states for environment understanding, task planning, and execution feedback [ 56 , 57 , 58 ] . Multimodal QA benchmarks evaluate perception, knowledge, and reasoning from images, videos, or other visual inputs [ 59 , 60 , 61 , 62 , 63 ] . Recent scientific benchmarks further cover chemical and materials experiment understanding, experiment video reasoning, laboratory embodied interaction, and robotic laboratory simulation [ 29 , 30 , 64 , 65 , 66 ] . However, benchmarks for the execution stage of SDCL-automated devices remain limited, as existing studies mainly address execution-process anomaly detection [ 26 , 27 ] or laboratory safety reasoning [ 28 ] . As shown in Table 1 , BEAKER instead targets visual contexts in real chemical experiments and jointly evaluates Actionability, Knowledge, Experimentation, and Reasoning, assessing whether multimodal embodied brains can support automated SDCL execution. Table 1: Comparison with related scientific and laboratory benchmarks. Scale denotes the primary evaluation unit of each work: QA for question-answering samples, tasks for embodied or robotic tasks, pairs for image-text pairs, imgs for images, and Sim. env. for simulation environments. ✓ , ✗ , and △ \triangle denote full, no, and partial coverage, respectively. Human indicates whether all questions and annotations are authored by human experts without LLM/AI-assisted generation or annotation. Benchmark Scale SDCL Real Image Video Action. Know. Exper. Reason. Human MaCBench [ 29 ] 1.1k+ QA △ \triangle ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗ ✓ △ \triangle ✓ ✓ ExpVid [ 30 ] 7.8k QA △ \triangle ✓ ✗ ✓ ✗ ✓ ✓ ✓ △ \triangle LabUtopia [ 64 ] 30 tasks △ \triangle ✗ ✓ ✗ △ \triangle ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ AutoBio [ 65 ] 16 tasks ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ △ \triangle ✓ ✓ △ \triangle ✓ Chemistry3D [ 66 ] Sim. env. △ \triangle ✗ ✓ ✗ △ \triangle ✓ ✓ △ \triangle ✓ SDCL Visual Anomaly Dataset [ 26 ] 2.8k pairs ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗ △ \triangle ✓ ✓ ✓ VLM-based Anomaly Detection [ 27 ] 1.0k imgs ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗ △ \triangle ✓ ✓ ✓ LabShield [ 28 ] 1.4k QA ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✗ BEAKER (Ours) 1.0k QA ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ 3 BEAKER 3.1 Design Principles Autonomous execution in SDCLs requires an embodied brain to close the loop from visual perception to physical action within chemically grounded contexts. Drawing on the classical sense-plan-act paradigm in robotics [ 67 , 68 ] and its recent extension to language-grounded embodied agents [ 69 , 70 ] , we decompose SDCL execution into four capability dimensions spanning low-level perception to high-level inference, each targeting distinct judgments required in real chemical experiments. Actionability. Actionability evaluates whether an MLLM can translate laboratory observations into physically actionable affordances and trajectories, which requires identifying operable regions, feasible interactions, and action-relevant motion paths under laboratory constraints. Knowledge. Reliable action presupposes accurate recognition of laboratory entities and awareness of procedural norms. This dimension evaluates whether a model can identify apparatus and reagents, understand their current states (e.g., liquid phase, precipitate formation, color changes), and judge whether an observed setup conforms to standard experimental practice. Experimentation. An embodied brain must also understand experimental operations as procedural processes [ 71 ] . Experimentation evaluates whether a model can recognize ongoing operations, understand apparatus connections, infer procedural intent, and track step-level progress. Reasoning. Chemical experiments require models to integrate visual evidence, experimental context, and domain knowledge to infer state changes, causal relationships, and experimental outcomes [ 30 ] . This dimension evaluates whether a model can reason over temporal observations of varying lengths and interpret experimental results from accumulated evidence, which is essential for closing the decision loop in autonomous SDCL workflows. 3.2 Benchmark Construction Expert-Curated Data Collection. All visual data in BEAKER is collected and filtered entirely by domain experts. For images, we survey publicly available chemical laboratory datasets across academic repositories and community platforms, identifying 12 representative sources covering diverse real-world laboratory scenes (see Appendix A ). Chemistry experts screen 11,128 candidate images and retain 883 that reflect realistic execution contexts: 275 simple images featuring a single apparatus or reagent against a clean background, and 608 complex images involving cluttered environments, multi-step setups, or active experimenter operations. Two senior embodied experts then verify that all retained images are suitable for embodied task design. Many images adopt first-person or experiment-execution viewpoints, resembling the visual inputs of automated devices in real SDCL execution. Figure 2: Overview of BEAKER construction and task examples. Top: the four-stage expert-curated pipeline of data collection, expert curation, QA authoring, and quality control. Bottom: examples of the four capability dimensions with the input, question, Ground Truth (GT), and GPT-5.4 [ 72 ] prediction. For videos, 334 short clips (4 s each) are extracted from the egocentric IBM Lab Actions dataset [ 73 ] ; 200 long experimental recordings (average duration ∼ \sim 9 min) with accompanying expert-authored transcripts are curated from the Journal of Visualized Experiments (JoVE) Chemistry collection [ 74 ] ; and mid-length clips are derived from these long videos via a semantic segmentation pipeline (FFmpeg [ 75 ] for audio extraction, Whisper [ 76 ] for timestamped transcription, and boundary detection between individual experimental steps), producing 1,753 candidate segments, of which experts retain 200 semantically complete clips (average duration ∼ \sim 50 s). Whisper only provides speech timestamps for proposing candidate segments; it is not involved in sample selection, question authoring, or annotation, all of which are performed by human experts. In total, the curated data pool comprises 883 images and 734 video clips. Ten chemistry experts then author detailed free-form captions for every item, describing apparatus, reagent states, ongoing operations, and safety-relevant details, yielding 1,617 expert-authored captions. For mid-length and long videos, the JoVE narration transcripts are not directly applicable to constructing BEAKER’s QA data, so experts combine each clip with its transcript to write captions tailored to this benchmark. Expert Annotation and QA Design. Recent studies show that benchmarks generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce systematic self-bias [ 77 ] and that LLM evaluators exhibit self-preference [ 78 ] . To reduce reliance on model-generated supervision, all benchmark questions and reference answers are authored and reviewed by human domain experts, without AI-assisted question or answer generation. Our annotation team comprises 10 chemistry experts, who ensure scientific correctness and domain accuracy, and 12 embodied experts, who verify operational relevance and feasibility from a robotic execution perspective. Two senior embodied experts coordinate overall quality control; the remaining 10 are each paired with one chemistry expert to form 10 interdisciplinary annotation groups. To ensure balanced task coverage while minimizing redundant annotations, each group receives the full curated data pool along with a task-type allocation matrix (see Appendix C ) specifying its question quota per category. Groups independently select suitable data items and design 150 QA samples each, yielding an initial pool of 1,500 candidate questions across 11 task types. Because all groups draw from the same pool, visually rich items may be selected by multiple groups; the allocation matrix steers these groups toward different task types for the same item, increasing per-item competency diversity rather than redundancy. To calibrate quality and difficulty, we apply a cross-group blind-review protocol inspired by expert-validation methodologies [ 79 ] . Each group’s 150 questions are distributed to two non-originating groups, whose members independently attempt every question without access to the ground-truth answer and evaluate it on four criteria: (i) scientific correctness, (ii) embodied operational relevance, (iii) difficulty calibration, and (iv) answer unambiguity. Reviewers also flag semantic duplicates , i.e., questions from different groups that target the same data item and competency, retaining only the highest-rated variant. Flagged questions enter a consensus adjudication round moderated by the two senior embodied experts, in which the originating and reviewing groups jointly decide whether to revise or discard each item. A question is discarded if it is answerable through surface-level visual cues alone ( e.g. , “ What is the color of the rubber-bulb pipette the lab worker is holding? ”), reduces to a trivial binary judgment without diagnostic value, demands excessively specialized knowledge beyond graduate-level chemistry, or lacks grounding in embodied execution contexts. Through this process, 500 questions (33.3%) are removed, and the remaining 1,000 constitute the final BEAKER benchmark, drawn from 410 images (152 simple, 258 complex) and 195 short, 125 mid-length, and 80 long videos. Fig. 2 illustrates this pipeline with task examples, and Fig. 3 summarizes the resulting statistics. The image tasks (600 samples) include two spatial tasks, Affordance Grounding (AFF) and Trajectory Planning (TRAJ), with 150 samples each annotated using the Computer Vision Annotation Tool (CVAT) [ 80 ] : AFF follows the point-and-box protocol of RoboBrain 2.0 [ 15 ] , with fine-grained boxes on precise regions such as stopcock tips and pipette nozzles, and TRAJ is annotated as ordered keypoint sequences. They also include five Multiple-Choice Question (MCQ) categories with 60 samples each (20 simple- and 40 complex-image questions): Equipment and Reagent Identification (ERI), Experimental Safety and Standardization (ESS), State Recognition (SR), Experimental Apparatus Setup (EAS), and Experimental Operations (EOP). The video tasks (400 samples) comprise Temporal Sequence Reasoning (TSR; 150 MCQs), evaluated separately on short, mid-length, and long videos as S-TSR, M-TSR, and L-TSR; Short-Video Operation Reasoning (SVOR; 125 MCQs); Mid-Video Task-Step Reasoning (MVTS; 75 MCQs); and Long-Video Experimental Procedure Reasoning (LVPR; 50 fill-in-the-blank questions requiring domain-specific phrases). The entire pipeline, from data screening through captioning, question authoring, and cross-group validation, spans about 1,200 expert-hours. Even for tasks that overlap with general embodied benchmarks, all questions are grounded in chemical laboratory execution contexts, so BEAKER evaluates domain-specific understanding rather than general visual competence. On the retained AFF questions, mean box Intersection over Union (IoU) reaches 86.9% and bidirectional point-in-region agreement reaches 100.0%; on the retained TRAJ questions, the mean trajectory agreement score is 85.6/100 (150 questions per task). All models are evaluated in a single-turn QA setting with standardized task-specific prompts and output formats (Appendix F ) and scored with task-specific metrics (Appendix E ). When configurable, the temperature is set to 0.7. All images are input at their original resolution. Short and mid-length videos are represented by 8 and 32 sampled frames, respectively, and long videos by 128 frames arranged into 32 four-frame grids (see Section 4.6 for a frame sampling ablation).
